original: Sun Tzŭ said: The art of war is of vital importance to the State.
plain: Sun Tzu said: Warfare is critically important to the state.
notes: 'The State' means the ruler's realm or kingdom, not a modern nation-state. 'Sun Tzŭ' is Giles's spelling of Sunzi ('Master Sun'). 'Art of war' here means the conduct of war, not a work of art.

original: It is a matter of life and death, a road either to safety or to ruin. Hence it is a subject of inquiry which can on no account be neglected.
plain: It decides life or death, survival or ruin. So it must be studied, and can never be ignored.

original: The art of war, then, is governed by five constant factors, to be taken into account in one’s deliberations, when seeking to determine the conditions obtaining in the field.
plain: Warfare is shaped by five constant factors. Weigh them carefully when working out the conditions you face in the field.
notes: 'Conditions obtaining in the field' is Victorian phrasing for 'the situation as it actually stands'.

original: These are: (1) The Moral Law; (2) Heaven; (3) Earth; (4) The Commander; (5) Method and discipline.
plain: The five are: (1) the Moral Law; (2) Heaven; (3) Earth; (4) the Commander; (5) Method and discipline.
notes: Each term is Giles's rendering of a single Chinese word and is defined in the next few points. 'Moral Law' translates dao (the Way); see I.5-6. 'Heaven' means weather, time and season, not the afterlife (I.7). 'Earth' means ground and distance (I.8).

original: The Moral Law causes the people to be in complete accord with their ruler, so that they will follow him regardless of their lives, undismayed by any danger.
plain: The Moral Law is what makes the people fully united with their ruler, so that they will follow him even at the cost of their lives, without fear of danger.
notes: Giles merges two points here. 'The Moral Law' translates dao, usually rendered 'the Way'. It may mean moral rightness, good government, or simply shared purpose between people and ruler - translators disagree, and Giles's phrase leans moral. The rewrite keeps his wording rather than choosing.

original: Heaven signifies night and day, cold and heat, times and seasons.
plain: Heaven means night and day, cold and heat, the timing of things and the seasons.
notes: 'Heaven' here is about weather and time, not religion.

original: Earth comprises distances, great and small; danger and security; open ground and narrow passes; the chances of life and death.
plain: Earth covers distances, short and long; danger and safety; open country and narrow passes; and the odds of living or dying.
notes: 'Earth' is the ground and its effect on survival - terrain, distance and position.

original: The Commander stands for the virtues of wisdom, sincerity, benevolence, courage and strictness.
plain: The Commander stands for the qualities of wisdom, sincerity, kindness, courage and strictness.
notes: 'Benevolence' is a Confucian-tinged word for humane care towards others. 'Sincerity' may also be read as trustworthiness.

original: By Method and discipline are to be understood the marshalling of the army in its proper subdivisions, the gradations of rank among the officers, the maintenance of roads by which supplies may reach the army, and the control of military expenditure.
plain: Method and discipline means organising the army into its proper units, setting the ranks of officers, keeping open the roads that bring supplies, and controlling military spending.
notes: 'Marshalling' means arranging troops in order. This factor covers organisation, logistics and budget, not just obedience.

original: These five heads should be familiar to every general: he who knows them will be victorious; he who knows them not will fail.
plain: Every general should know these five factors well. Whoever knows them will win; whoever does not will fail.
notes: 'Heads' means headings or categories.

original: Therefore, in your deliberations, when seeking to determine the military conditions, let them be made the basis of a comparison, in this wise:—
plain: So, when you are working out the military situation, use these factors as the basis for comparing the two sides, as follows:
notes: 'In this wise' is old phrasing for 'in this way' or 'as follows'.

original:
(1) Which of the two sovereigns is imbued with the Moral law?
(2) Which of the two generals has most ability?
(3) With whom lie the advantages derived from Heaven and Earth?
(4) On which side is discipline most rigorously enforced?
(5) Which army is the stronger?
(6) On which side are officers and men more highly trained?
(7) In which army is there the greater constancy both in reward and punishment?
plain:
(1) Which of the two rulers has the Moral Law?
(2) Which of the two generals is more capable?
(3) Which side has the advantages of Heaven and Earth (weather, timing and ground)?
(4) Which side enforces discipline more strictly?
(5) Which army is stronger?
(6) Which side has better-trained officers and soldiers?
(7) Which army is more consistent in rewarding and punishing?
notes: 'Imbued with the Moral law' depends on how 'Moral Law' is read (see I.5-6): it may mean moral authority or simply having the people united behind him. 'Constancy' means consistency.

original: By means of these seven considerations I can forecast victory or defeat.
plain: Using these seven comparisons, I can predict victory or defeat.

original: The general that hearkens to my counsel and acts upon it, will conquer: let such a one be retained in command! The general that hearkens not to my counsel nor acts upon it, will suffer defeat:—let such a one be dismissed!
plain: A general who listens to my advice and acts on it will win - keep him in command. A general who does not listen or act on it will be defeated - dismiss him.
notes: Ambiguous in the Chinese. Giles reads it as advice to a ruler about which generals to keep. Other translators read it as Sun Tzu saying he himself will stay if his advice is followed and leave if not. Kept to Giles's reading.

original: While heeding the profit of my counsel, avail yourself also of any helpful circumstances over and beyond the ordinary rules.
plain: While making use of my advice, also take advantage of any helpful circumstances beyond the usual rules.
notes: 'Heeding the profit of my counsel' means 'benefiting from my advice'.

original: According as circumstances are favourable, one should modify one’s plans.
plain: Change your plans to suit whatever circumstances favour you.
notes: 'According as circumstances are favourable' means 'in line with what the situation offers'. The Chinese term behind this passage is often linked to shi (strategic advantage or momentum).

original: All warfare is based on deception.
plain: All warfare depends on deception.
notes: Short and absolute in Giles. Some translators soften 'deception' to misdirection or 'the way of guile'. The scope of the claim is debated.

original: Hence, when able to attack, we must seem unable; when using our forces, we must seem inactive; when we are near, we must make the enemy believe we are far away; when far away, we must make him believe we are near.
plain: So when you can attack, look as if you cannot. When you are using your forces, look inactive. When you are close, make the enemy think you are far away; when far away, make him think you are close.

original: Hold out baits to entice the enemy. Feign disorder, and crush him.
plain: Offer baits to lure the enemy in. Pretend to be in disorder, then crush him.

original: If he is secure at all points, be prepared for him. If he is in superior strength, evade him.
plain: If he is secure everywhere, be ready for him. If he is stronger, avoid him.
notes: 'Be prepared for him' may mean prepare defensively against him, or prepare carefully before engaging. Left open.

original: If your opponent is of choleric temper, seek to irritate him. Pretend to be weak, that he may grow arrogant.
plain: If your opponent is hot-tempered, try to provoke him. Pretend to be weak, so that he becomes arrogant.
notes: 'Choleric' is old medical language for quick-tempered or easily angered.

original: If he is taking his ease, give him no rest. If his forces are united, separate them.
plain: If he is resting, give him no rest. If his forces are united, split them up.
notes: 'Taking his ease' means resting or relaxed.

original: Attack him where he is unprepared, appear where you are not expected.
plain: Attack him where he is unprepared. Turn up where you are not expected.

original: These military devices, leading to victory, must not be divulged beforehand.
plain: These military tricks, which lead to victory, must not be revealed in advance.
notes: 'Devices' means tactics or stratagems. 'Divulged' means revealed. Some read 'must not be divulged beforehand' as 'cannot be fixed in advance' - they depend on the moment.

original: Now the general who wins a battle makes many calculations in his temple ere the battle is fought. The general who loses a battle makes but few calculations beforehand. Thus do many calculations lead to victory, and few calculations to defeat: how much more no calculation at all! It is by attention to this point that I can foresee who is likely to win or lose.
plain: The general who wins makes many calculations in his temple before the battle. The general who loses makes few. Many calculations lead to victory and few to defeat - and none at all is worse still. By looking at this, I can foresee who is likely to win or lose.
notes: 'Temple' refers to the ancestral temple where war councils were held. 'Ere' means before. 'Calculations' may mean counting tokens to tally advantages, not arithmetic.

original: Sun Tzŭ said: In the operations of war, where there are in the field a thousand swift chariots, as many heavy chariots, and a hundred thousand mail-clad soldiers, with provisions enough to carry them a thousand li, the expenditure at home and at the front, including entertainment of guests, small items such as glue and paint, and sums spent on chariots and armour, will reach the total of a thousand ounces of silver per day. Such is the cost of raising an army of 100,000 men.
plain: Sun Tzu said: Suppose a war involves a thousand fast chariots, a thousand heavy chariots and a hundred thousand armoured soldiers, with enough supplies to carry them a thousand li. Spending at home and at the front - including hosting visitors, small items like glue and paint, and money for chariots and armour - will come to a thousand ounces of silver a day. That is the cost of raising an army of 100,000 men.
notes: 'Li' is a Chinese unit of distance, a few hundred metres (it varied over time). 'Mail-clad' means wearing armour. 'Entertainment of guests' likely means hosting envoys and advisers. The figures illustrate scale rather than an exact budget.

original: When you engage in actual fighting, if victory is long in coming, the men’s weapons will grow dull and their ardour will be damped. If you lay siege to a town, you will exhaust your strength.
plain: Once fighting starts, if victory is slow to come, the soldiers' weapons will get blunt and their enthusiasm will fade. If you besiege a town, you will wear out your strength.
notes: 'Ardour will be damped' means enthusiasm will be dampened.

original: Again, if the campaign is protracted, the resources of the State will not be equal to the strain.
plain: And if the campaign drags on, the state's resources will not be able to cope.
notes: 'Protracted' means drawn out.

original: Now, when your weapons are dulled, your ardour damped, your strength exhausted and your treasure spent, other chieftains will spring up to take advantage of your extremity. Then no man, however wise, will be able to avert the consequences that must ensue.
plain: Once your weapons are blunt, your enthusiasm gone, your strength used up and your money spent, other leaders will rise up to exploit your weakness. Then no one, however wise, will be able to prevent what follows.
notes: 'Chieftains' means rival rulers or warlords. 'Extremity' means a desperate state.

original: Thus, though we have heard of stupid haste in war, cleverness has never been seen associated with long delays.
plain: So although we have heard of war being rushed foolishly, no one has ever seen cleverness linked with long delays.
notes: A famous and debated line. Giles's version suggests haste can be stupid but delay is never clever. Some read it as 'a clumsy quick war is better than a clever long one'. Kept to Giles's balance.

original: There is no instance of a country having benefited from prolonged warfare.
plain: No country has ever gained from a long war.

original: It is only one who is thoroughly acquainted with the evils of war that can thoroughly understand the profitable way of carrying it on.
plain: Only someone who fully understands the harms of war can fully understand how to wage it to advantage.
notes: 'Profitable' means advantageous, not only financially.

original: The skilful soldier does not raise a second levy, neither are his supply-waggons loaded more than twice.
plain: A skilled soldier does not call up troops a second time, and does not load his supply wagons more than twice.
notes: 'Levy' means a conscription or call-up. The wagon line is usually read as: supplies go out once at the start and come back once at the end, with the army living off captured supplies in between. That reading is the commentators', not stated in the text.

original: Bring war material with you from home, but forage on the enemy. Thus the army will have food enough for its needs.
plain: Bring your equipment from home, but take food from the enemy. That way the army will have enough to eat.
notes: 'Forage on the enemy' means gather or seize supplies from enemy territory.

original: Poverty of the State exchequer causes an army to be maintained by contributions from a distance. Contributing to maintain an army at a distance causes the people to be impoverished.
plain: When the state treasury is poor, the army ends up being supplied from far away. Supplying an army from far away makes the people poor.
notes: 'Exchequer' means treasury. Giles's order of cause is odd: many translators read it the other way round - supplying an army over a long distance is what makes the state poor. The rewrite keeps Giles's order.

original: On the other hand, the proximity of an army causes prices to go up; and high prices cause the people’s substance to be drained away.
plain: On the other hand, when an army is nearby, prices go up, and high prices drain away people's wealth.
notes: 'Substance' means wealth or livelihood.

original: When their substance is drained away, the peasantry will be afflicted by heavy exactions.
plain: When their wealth is drained, the farming population will be hit by heavy demands.
notes: 'Exactions' means levies, taxes or forced contributions.

original: With this loss of substance and exhaustion of strength, the homes of the people will be stripped bare, and three-tenths of their incomes will be dissipated; while Government expenses for broken chariots, worn-out horses, breast-plates and helmets, bows and arrows, spears and shields, protective mantlets, draught-oxen and heavy waggons, will amount to four-tenths of its total revenue.
plain: With this loss of wealth and strength, people's homes will be stripped bare and three-tenths of their income will be lost. Meanwhile the government's costs for broken chariots, worn-out horses, breastplates and helmets, bows and arrows, spears and shields, protective screens, draught oxen and heavy wagons will come to four-tenths of its total revenue.
notes: Giles merges two points. Other translations give different fractions, so treat the figures as illustrative. 'Mantlets' are movable protective screens. 'Draught-oxen' are oxen used to pull loads.

original: Hence a wise general makes a point of foraging on the enemy. One cartload of the enemy’s provisions is equivalent to twenty of one’s own, and likewise a single picul of his provender is equivalent to twenty from one’s own store.
plain: So a wise general makes a point of taking supplies from the enemy. One cartload of the enemy's provisions is worth twenty of your own, and one picul of his fodder is worth twenty from your own store.
notes: 'Picul' is a weight unit (Giles's term for a Chinese measure). 'Provender' means animal feed. The 'twenty to one' reflects the cost of transporting supplies over distance.

original: Now in order to kill the enemy, our men must be roused to anger; that there may be advantage from defeating the enemy, they must have their rewards.
plain: To get your men to kill the enemy, they must be stirred to anger. To make them gain something from defeating the enemy, they must be rewarded.
notes: The second clause can mean rewards motivate soldiers, or that captured goods should become rewards. The Chinese can carry both senses.

original: Therefore in chariot fighting, when ten or more chariots have been taken, those should be rewarded who took the first. Our own flags should be substituted for those of the enemy, and the chariots mingled and used in conjunction with ours. The captured soldiers should be kindly treated and kept.
plain: So in chariot fighting, when ten or more chariots have been captured, reward whoever took the first one. Replace the enemy's flags with your own, and mix the captured chariots in with yours and use them. Treat captured soldiers well and keep them.
notes: 'Kept' may mean held, looked after, or taken into your own force. Left open.

original: This is called, using the conquered foe to augment one’s own strength.
plain: This is called using a beaten enemy to add to your own strength.
notes: 'Augment' means increase.

original: In war, then, let your great object be victory, not lengthy campaigns.
plain: So in war, make victory your main aim - not long campaigns.

original: Thus it may be known that the leader of armies is the arbiter of the people’s fate, the man on whom it depends whether the nation shall be in peace or in peril.
plain: So it is clear that the leader of armies decides the people's fate. Whether the nation is at peace or in danger depends on him.
notes: 'Arbiter' means the one who decides. Some translators read 'the people's fate' as their lives (the 'master of life and death').

original: Sun Tzŭ said: In the practical art of war, the best thing of all is to take the enemy’s country whole and intact; to shatter and destroy it is not so good. So, too, it is better to capture an army entire than to destroy it, to capture a regiment, a detachment or a company entire than to destroy them.
plain: Sun Tzu said: In practice, the best thing of all in war is to take the enemy's country whole and undamaged; smashing and destroying it is second best. In the same way, it is better to capture an army whole than to destroy it - and better to capture a regiment, a detachment or a company whole than to destroy it.
notes: 'Regiment', 'detachment' and 'company' are Giles's European labels for Chinese unit sizes, not exact equivalents.

original: Hence to fight and conquer in all your battles is not supreme excellence; supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy’s resistance without fighting.
plain: So winning every battle you fight is not the highest skill. The highest skill is breaking the enemy's resistance without fighting.
notes: Often quoted as 'win without fighting'. The point ranks means; it does not say force is never used.

original: Thus the highest form of generalship is to baulk the enemy’s plans; the next best is to prevent the junction of the enemy’s forces; the next in order is to attack the enemy’s army in the field; and the worst policy of all is to besiege walled cities.
plain: So the best generalship is to defeat the enemy's plans. Next best is to stop his forces from joining up. Next is to attack his army in the field. Worst of all is to besiege walled cities.
notes: 'Baulk' means frustrate or block. 'Prevent the junction of the enemy's forces' is Giles's reading; most modern translators read this as 'disrupt his alliances'. Both are defensible from the Chinese.

original: The rule is, not to besiege walled cities if it can possibly be avoided. The preparation of mantlets, movable shelters, and various implements of war, will take up three whole months; and the piling up of mounds over against the walls will take three months more.
plain: The rule is: do not besiege walled cities if you can possibly avoid it. Preparing screens, movable shelters and siege equipment takes three full months, and building earth mounds against the walls takes another three.
notes: 'Mantlets' are protective screens. 'Mounds' are siege ramps built against the walls.

original: The general, unable to control his irritation, will launch his men to the assault like swarming ants, with the result that one-third of his men are slain, while the town still remains untaken. Such are the disastrous effects of a siege.
plain: The general, unable to control his frustration, sends his men to swarm the walls like ants. A third of them are killed and the town still has not fallen. That is how disastrous a siege can be.

original: Therefore the skilful leader subdues the enemy’s troops without any fighting; he captures their cities without laying siege to them; he overthrows their kingdom without lengthy operations in the field.
plain: So a skilled leader defeats the enemy's troops without fighting, takes their cities without besieging them, and overthrows their kingdom without long campaigns in the field.
notes: 'Subdues' means brings under control.

original: With his forces intact he will dispute the mastery of the Empire, and thus, without losing a man, his triumph will be complete. This is the method of attacking by stratagem.
plain: With his forces still whole, he will contest for supremacy over the empire, and so, without losing a man, his victory will be complete. This is the method of attacking by strategy.
notes: 'The Empire' is Giles's term for 'all under heaven' - the whole Chinese world of rival states, not a single empire. 'Dispute the mastery' means compete for supremacy. 'Stratagem' means a clever plan rather than force.

original: It is the rule in war, if our forces are ten to the enemy’s one, to surround him; if five to one, to attack him; if twice as numerous, to divide our army into two.
plain: The rule in war is: if you outnumber the enemy ten to one, surround him; if five to one, attack him; if two to one, split your army in two.
notes: The last clause is disputed: it may mean split your own army to attack from two sides, or split the enemy's army. Giles chooses your own army.

original: If equally matched, we can offer battle; if slightly inferior in numbers, we can avoid the enemy; if quite unequal in every way, we can flee from him.
plain: If evenly matched, you can give battle. If slightly outnumbered, you can avoid the enemy. If outclassed in every way, you can run from him.
notes: 'Offer battle' means be willing to fight.

original: Hence, though an obstinate fight may be made by a small force, in the end it must be captured by the larger force.
plain: So although a small force may put up a stubborn fight, in the end the larger force will capture it.
notes: 'Obstinate' means stubborn.

original: Now the general is the bulwark of the State: if the bulwark is complete at all points; the State will be strong; if the bulwark is defective, the State will be weak.
plain: The general is the protective wall of the state. If that wall is strong everywhere, the state will be strong; if it has weak spots, the state will be weak.
notes: 'Bulwark' means a defensive wall or protector.

original: There are three ways in which a ruler can bring misfortune upon his army:—
plain: There are three ways a ruler can bring trouble on his own army:

original: (1) By commanding the army to advance or to retreat, being ignorant of the fact that it cannot obey. This is called hobbling the army.
plain: (1) Ordering the army to advance or retreat without knowing that it is unable to. This is called hobbling the army.
notes: To 'hobble' is to tie a horse's legs so it cannot move freely.

original: (2) By attempting to govern an army in the same way as he administers a kingdom, being ignorant of the conditions which obtain in an army. This causes restlessness in the soldier’s minds.
plain: (2) Trying to run an army the same way he runs a kingdom, without understanding army conditions. This makes the soldiers restless.

original: (3) By employing the officers of his army without discrimination, through ignorance of the military principle of adaptation to circumstances. This shakes the confidence of the soldiers.
plain: (3) Appointing army officers without good judgement, because he does not understand the military principle of adapting to circumstances. This shakes the soldiers' confidence.
notes: Ambiguous. Giles reads it as the ruler employing officers poorly. Other versions read it as the ruler taking part in army command himself without understanding it. 'Without discrimination' means without discernment, not unfairness.

original: But when the army is restless and distrustful, trouble is sure to come from the other feudal princes. This is simply bringing anarchy into the army, and flinging victory away.
plain: Once the army is restless and distrustful, trouble from the other feudal lords is sure to follow. This simply brings chaos into the army and throws victory away.
notes: 'Feudal princes' means neighbouring lords or states who may take advantage.

original:
Thus we may know that there are five essentials for victory:
(1) He will win who knows when to fight and when not to fight.
(2) He will win who knows how to handle both superior and inferior forces.
(3) He will win whose army is animated by the same spirit throughout all its ranks.
(4) He will win who, prepared himself, waits to take the enemy unprepared.
(5) He will win who has military capacity and is not interfered with by the sovereign.
Victory lies in the knowledge of these five points.
plain:
So there are five essentials for victory:
(1) Whoever knows when to fight and when not to will win.
(2) Whoever knows how to handle both larger and smaller forces will win.
(3) Whoever has an army sharing the same spirit at every level will win.
(4) Whoever is prepared and waits to catch the enemy unprepared will win.
(5) Whoever is militarily capable and not interfered with by the ruler will win.
Victory lies in knowing these five points.
notes: 'Superior and inferior forces' most likely means larger and smaller numbers.

original: Hence the saying: If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles. If you know yourself but not the enemy, for every victory gained you will also suffer a defeat. If you know neither the enemy nor yourself, you will succumb in every battle.
plain: So it is said: if you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the outcome of a hundred battles. If you know yourself but not the enemy, for every victory you will also suffer a defeat. If you know neither the enemy nor yourself, you will lose every battle.
notes: Often misquoted as 'win a hundred battles'; Giles has 'need not fear the result'.

original: Sun Tzŭ said: The good fighters of old first put themselves beyond the possibility of defeat, and then waited for an opportunity of defeating the enemy.
plain: Sun Tzu said: Good fighters in the past first made themselves impossible to defeat, then waited for a chance to defeat the enemy.

original: To secure ourselves against defeat lies in our own hands, but the opportunity of defeating the enemy is provided by the enemy himself.
plain: Making ourselves safe from defeat is in our own hands, but the chance to defeat the enemy is given to us by the enemy himself.

original: Thus the good fighter is able to secure himself against defeat, but cannot make certain of defeating the enemy.
plain: So a good fighter can make himself safe from defeat, but cannot guarantee defeating the enemy.

original: Hence the saying: One may know how to conquer without being able to do it.
plain: So it is said: you can know how to win without being able to do it.
notes: Giles italicised 'know' and 'do' for emphasis; the markers are removed here.

original: Security against defeat implies defensive tactics; ability to defeat the enemy means taking the offensive.
plain: Being safe from defeat means defending. Being able to defeat the enemy means attacking.
notes: 'Implies' here means 'comes from' or 'calls for'.

original: Standing on the defensive indicates insufficient strength; attacking, a superabundance of strength.
plain: Defending is a sign of not having enough strength; attacking, of having more than enough.
notes: A known ambiguity. Giles reads it as what defence and attack reveal about strength. Many translators instead read it as advice: defend when you lack strength, attack when you have plenty. The excavated Yinqueshan manuscript has wording that reverses the line. Kept to Giles.

original: The general who is skilled in defence hides in the most secret recesses of the earth; he who is skilled in attack flashes forth from the topmost heights of heaven. Thus on the one hand we have ability to protect ourselves; on the other, a victory that is complete.
plain: The general skilled in defence hides in the deepest places of the earth; the one skilled in attack strikes from the highest point of heaven. So on one hand we can protect ourselves, and on the other we can win completely.
notes: 'Earth' and 'heaven' here are poetic images for total concealment and sudden, overwhelming attack, not literal places.

original: To see victory only when it is within the ken of the common herd is not the acme of excellence.
plain: Seeing a victory only when ordinary people can see it too is not the height of skill.
notes: 'Within the ken of the common herd' means within the understanding of ordinary people. 'Acme' means peak.

original: Neither is it the acme of excellence if you fight and conquer and the whole Empire says, “Well done!”
plain: Nor is it the height of skill if you fight, win, and the whole empire says 'Well done!'
notes: 'The Empire' means the whole Chinese world (see III.7).

original: To lift an autumn hair is no sign of great strength; to see sun and moon is no sign of sharp sight; to hear the noise of thunder is no sign of a quick ear.
plain: Lifting an autumn hair does not show great strength; seeing the sun and moon does not show sharp eyesight; hearing thunder does not show good hearing.
notes: An 'autumn hair' is the fine new fur an animal grows in autumn - a standard image for something very light.

original: What the ancients called a clever fighter is one who not only wins, but excels in winning with ease.
plain: What people of old called a clever fighter is one who not only wins, but wins easily.

original: Hence his victories bring him neither reputation for wisdom nor credit for courage.
plain: So his victories earn him no reputation for wisdom and no credit for courage.
notes: Because his wins look easy, nobody sees the skill behind them.

original: He wins his battles by making no mistakes. Making no mistakes is what establishes the certainty of victory, for it means conquering an enemy that is already defeated.
plain: He wins his battles by making no mistakes. Making no mistakes is what makes victory certain, because it means defeating an enemy who is already beaten.

original: Hence the skilful fighter puts himself into a position which makes defeat impossible, and does not miss the moment for defeating the enemy.
plain: So the skilled fighter puts himself in a position where defeat is impossible, and does not miss the moment to defeat the enemy.

original: Thus it is that in war the victorious strategist only seeks battle after the victory has been won, whereas he who is destined to defeat first fights and afterwards looks for victory.
plain: So in war the victorious strategist only looks for battle after the victory has already been won, while the one bound to lose fights first and then looks for victory.
notes: 'Victory has been won' means the conditions for winning are already in place before the fighting.

original: The consummate leader cultivates the moral law, and strictly adheres to method and discipline; thus it is in his power to control success.
plain: The accomplished leader cultivates the Moral Law and sticks firmly to method and discipline. That way, success is within his control.
notes: 'Moral law' and 'method and discipline' refer back to the five factors in I.4. 'Consummate' means highly skilled.

original: In respect of military method, we have, firstly, Measurement; secondly, Estimation of quantity; thirdly, Calculation; fourthly, Balancing of chances; fifthly, Victory.
plain: In military method there is first Measurement, second Estimating quantity, third Calculation, fourth Weighing the odds, and fifth Victory.
notes: These are a chain of steps. 'Measurement' likely means measuring ground and distance; 'estimation of quantity' means resources and numbers. The exact meaning of each Chinese term is debated.

original: Measurement owes its existence to Earth; Estimation of quantity to Measurement; Calculation to Estimation of quantity; Balancing of chances to Calculation; and Victory to Balancing of chances.
plain: Measurement comes from Earth; estimating quantity comes from measurement; calculation from estimating quantity; weighing the odds from calculation; and victory from weighing the odds.
notes: 'Earth' is the terrain factor from I.8. Each step depends on the one before.

original: A victorious army opposed to a routed one, is as a pound’s weight placed in the scale against a single grain.
plain: A winning army set against a broken one is like a pound weight on the scales against a single grain.
notes: 'Routed' means defeated and fleeing in disorder. The original uses Chinese weight units; Giles substitutes 'pound' and 'grain'.

original: The onrush of a conquering force is like the bursting of pent-up waters into a chasm a thousand fathoms deep. So much for tactical dispositions.
plain: The charge of a winning army is like dammed-up water bursting into a gorge a thousand fathoms deep. That is all on tactical dispositions.
notes: 'Fathom' is an old unit of about 1.8 metres - here simply 'very deep'. 'Tactical dispositions' means how forces are positioned and arranged.

original: Sun Tzŭ said: The control of a large force is the same principle as the control of a few men: it is merely a question of dividing up their numbers.
plain: Sun Tzu said: Controlling a large force works on the same principle as controlling a few men: it is just a matter of dividing them into units.

original: Fighting with a large army under your command is nowise different from fighting with a small one: it is merely a question of instituting signs and signals.
plain: Fighting with a large army is no different from fighting with a small one: it is just a matter of setting up signs and signals.
notes: 'Nowise' means in no way. The Chinese terms behind 'signs and signals' are often read as formations and signals (flags and drums) - more than just communication.

original: To ensure that your whole host may withstand the brunt of the enemy’s attack and remain unshaken—this is effected by manœuvers direct and indirect.
plain: Making sure your whole army can take the full force of an enemy attack and stay unbroken is done through direct and indirect manoeuvres.
notes: 'Direct and indirect' translate zheng and qi, a key pair: the expected, conventional move and the surprising, unconventional one. Other renderings are 'orthodox and unorthodox' or 'regular and extraordinary'.

original: That the impact of your army may be like a grindstone dashed against an egg—this is effected by the science of weak points and strong.
plain: Making your army hit like a grindstone thrown against an egg is done through the science of weak points and strong ones.
notes: The weak/strong pair is the subject of Chapter VI. Also rendered 'empty and full' or 'void and solid'.

original: In all fighting, the direct method may be used for joining battle, but indirect methods will be needed in order to secure victory.
plain: In all fighting, the direct method can be used to engage, but indirect methods are needed to win.
notes: See V.3 on direct and indirect.

original: Indirect tactics, efficiently applied, are inexhaustible as Heaven and Earth, unending as the flow of rivers and streams; like the sun and moon, they end but to begin anew; like the four seasons, they pass away but to return once more.
plain: Indirect tactics, used well, are as endless as Heaven and Earth, as unending as rivers and streams. Like the sun and moon, they end only to begin again; like the four seasons, they pass only to return.
notes: Here 'Heaven and Earth' means the whole natural world, not the technical factors of I.7-8.

original: There are not more than five musical notes, yet the combinations of these five give rise to more melodies than can ever be heard.
plain: There are only five musical notes, yet their combinations make more tunes than could ever be heard.
notes: Chinese music used a five-note (pentatonic) scale.

original: There are not more than five primary colours (blue, yellow, red, white, and black), yet in combination they produce more hues than can ever be seen.
plain: There are only five primary colours (blue, yellow, red, white and black), yet together they make more shades than could ever be seen.
notes: These are the five traditional Chinese colours, not the modern primary colours.

original: There are not more than five cardinal tastes (sour, acrid, salt, sweet, bitter), yet combinations of them yield more flavours than can ever be tasted.
plain: There are only five basic tastes (sour, sharp, salty, sweet and bitter), yet their combinations make more flavours than could ever be tasted.
notes: 'Acrid' here means pungent or sharp, as in spice.

original: In battle, there are not more than two methods of attack—the direct and the indirect; yet these two in combination give rise to an endless series of manœuvers.
plain: In battle there are only two methods of attack - direct and indirect - yet together they produce an endless series of manoeuvres.

original: The direct and the indirect lead on to each other in turn. It is like moving in a circle—you never come to an end. Who can exhaust the possibilities of their combination?
plain: Direct and indirect keep turning into each other. It is like going round a circle - you never reach the end. Who could exhaust the ways they can be combined?
notes: The point is that the expected move and the surprise move can swap roles.

original: The onset of troops is like the rush of a torrent which will even roll stones along in its course.
plain: The charge of troops is like a rushing torrent that even rolls stones along with it.
notes: 'Onset' means charge or attack.

original: The quality of decision is like the well-timed swoop of a falcon which enables it to strike and destroy its victim.
plain: Good decision-making is like the perfectly timed swoop of a falcon that lets it strike and kill its prey.
notes: 'The quality of decision' is Giles's phrase; others render the underlying idea as timing, or the short, sharp release of force at the right distance.

original: Therefore the good fighter will be terrible in his onset, and prompt in his decision.
plain: So the good fighter will be fearsome in his charge and quick in his decisions.
notes: 'Terrible' means fearsome, not bad.

original: Energy may be likened to the bending of a crossbow; decision, to the releasing of the trigger.
plain: Energy is like drawing back a crossbow; decision is like pulling the trigger.
notes: 'Energy' translates shi, often rendered 'strategic advantage', 'momentum' or 'potential' - stored force waiting to be released.

original: Amid the turmoil and tumult of battle, there may be seeming disorder and yet no real disorder at all; amid confusion and chaos, your array may be without head or tail, yet it will be proof against defeat.
plain: Amid the noise and chaos of battle, there can be apparent disorder without real disorder. Amid confusion, your formation may seem to have no front or rear, yet it cannot be defeated.
notes: 'Without head or tail' means without a clear front and back - possibly a round formation.

original: Simulated disorder postulates perfect discipline; simulated fear postulates courage; simulated weakness postulates strength.
plain: Faking disorder requires perfect discipline; faking fear requires courage; faking weakness requires strength.
notes: 'Postulates' means requires or presupposes. Also read as: disorder arises from order, fear from courage, weakness from strength.

original: Hiding order beneath the cloak of disorder is simply a question of subdivision; concealing courage under a show of timidity presupposes a fund of latent energy; masking strength with weakness is to be effected by tactical dispositions.
plain: Hiding order under a show of disorder is simply a matter of dividing up your forces. Hiding courage under a show of timidity requires a reserve of hidden energy. Hiding strength under weakness is done through tactical positioning.
notes: 'Subdivision' refers back to V.1 (organising into units). 'Latent energy' refers to shi (see V.15).

original: Thus one who is skilful at keeping the enemy on the move maintains deceitful appearances, according to which the enemy will act. He sacrifices something, that the enemy may snatch at it.
plain: So someone skilled at keeping the enemy moving puts on deceptive appearances that the enemy will act on. He gives something up so that the enemy will grab it.

original: By holding out baits, he keeps him on the march; then with a body of picked men he lies in wait for him.
plain: By offering baits he keeps the enemy on the move; then he waits in ambush for him with a body of picked troops.
notes: 'Picked men' means selected, elite troops.

original: The clever combatant looks to the effect of combined energy, and does not require too much from individuals. Hence his ability to pick out the right men and utilise combined energy.
plain: The clever fighter relies on the effect of combined energy and does not demand too much from individuals. That is how he can pick the right people and make use of combined energy.
notes: 'Combined energy' translates shi again (see V.15). Some read the second sentence as 'he chooses the right people and lets the situation do the work'.

original: When he utilises combined energy, his fighting men become as it were like unto rolling logs or stones. For it is the nature of a log or stone to remain motionless on level ground, and to move when on a slope; if four-cornered, to come to a standstill, but if round-shaped, to go rolling down.
plain: When he uses combined energy, his fighters become like rolling logs or stones. Logs and stones stay still on flat ground and move on a slope; if square, they stop, but if round, they roll down.
notes: 'Like unto' is old phrasing for 'like'.

original: Thus the energy developed by good fighting men is as the momentum of a round stone rolled down a mountain thousands of feet in height. So much on the subject of energy.
plain: So the energy produced by good fighters is like the momentum of a round stone rolled down a mountain thousands of feet high. That is all on energy.
notes: The image is about position creating force: the stone's power comes from where it is placed, not its own effort.

original: Sun Tzŭ said: Whoever is first in the field and awaits the coming of the enemy, will be fresh for the fight; whoever is second in the field and has to hasten to battle, will arrive exhausted.
plain: Sun Tzu said: Whoever arrives first on the battlefield and waits for the enemy will be fresh for the fight. Whoever arrives second and has to rush into battle will be worn out.

original: Therefore the clever combatant imposes his will on the enemy, but does not allow the enemy’s will to be imposed on him.
plain: So the clever fighter imposes his will on the enemy and does not let the enemy impose his will on him.
notes: Often rendered 'he moves the enemy and is not moved by him' - about holding the initiative.

original: By holding out advantages to him, he can cause the enemy to approach of his own accord; or, by inflicting damage, he can make it impossible for the enemy to draw near.
plain: By offering the enemy advantages, he can get him to come forward of his own accord. Or, by doing him damage, he can make it impossible for him to come near.

original: If the enemy is taking his ease, he can harass him; if well supplied with food, he can starve him out; if quietly encamped, he can force him to move.
plain: If the enemy is resting, he can harass him. If the enemy is well supplied with food, he can starve him out. If the enemy is calmly camped, he can force him to move.

original: Appear at points which the enemy must hasten to defend; march swiftly to places where you are not expected.
plain: Turn up at points the enemy must rush to defend. March quickly to places where you are not expected.
notes: The Chinese is compressed and has variant readings; some versions read the first clause as 'appear where he cannot hurry to'. Kept to Giles.

original: An army may march great distances without distress, if it marches through country where the enemy is not.
plain: An army can march long distances without hardship if it goes through country where the enemy is not.

original: You can be sure of succeeding in your attacks if you only attack places which are undefended.You can ensure the safety of your defence if you only hold positions that cannot be attacked.
plain: You can be sure your attacks will succeed if you only attack places that are not defended. You can make sure your defence is safe if you only hold positions that cannot be attacked.
notes: Giles's text runs the two sentences together without a space ('undefended.You'); the original is kept exactly. 'Cannot be attacked' is often read as 'that the enemy will not attack'.

original: Hence that general is skilful in attack whose opponent does not know what to defend; and he is skilful in defence whose opponent does not know what to attack.
plain: So a general is skilled in attack when his opponent does not know what to defend, and skilled in defence when his opponent does not know what to attack.

original: O divine art of subtlety and secrecy! Through you we learn to be invisible, through you inaudible; and hence we can hold the enemy’s fate in our hands.
plain: Oh, the divine art of subtlety and secrecy! Through it we learn to be invisible and silent, and so we can hold the enemy's fate in our hands.
notes: 'O divine art' is Giles's poetic flourish. The Chinese is more like 'subtle, subtle - to the point of formlessness; mysterious, mysterious - to the point of soundlessness'.

original: You may advance and be absolutely irresistible, if you make for the enemy’s weak points; you may retire and be safe from pursuit if your movements are more rapid than those of the enemy.
plain: You can advance and be unstoppable if you head for the enemy's weak points. You can withdraw and be safe from pursuit if you move faster than the enemy.

original: If we wish to fight, the enemy can be forced to an engagement even though he be sheltered behind a high rampart and a deep ditch. All we need do is attack some other place that he will be obliged to relieve.
plain: If we want to fight, we can force the enemy into battle even if he is sheltered behind a high wall and a deep ditch. All we need to do is attack some other place he will have to come and relieve.
notes: 'Rampart' means a defensive earth wall. 'Relieve' means come to the aid of.

original: If we do not wish to fight, we can prevent the enemy from engaging us even though the lines of our encampment be merely traced out on the ground. All we need do is to throw something odd and unaccountable in his way.
plain: If we do not want to fight, we can stop the enemy from engaging us even if our camp is only marked out on the ground. All we need to do is put something strange and puzzling in his way.
notes: 'Throw something odd and unaccountable in his way' is Giles's reading. Other translators read it as 'divert him from where he is going'. The Chinese supports both.

original: By discovering the enemy’s dispositions and remaining invisible ourselves, we can keep our forces concentrated, while the enemy’s must be divided.
plain: By finding out the enemy's positions while staying hidden ourselves, we can keep our forces together while the enemy has to split his.
notes: 'Dispositions' means how forces are arranged and positioned.

original: We can form a single united body, while the enemy must split up into fractions. Hence there will be a whole pitted against separate parts of a whole, which means that we shall be many to the enemy’s few.
plain: We can form one united body while the enemy breaks into fragments. Then it will be a whole against separate parts of a whole, which means we will be many against the enemy's few.

original: And if we are able thus to attack an inferior force with a superior one, our opponents will be in dire straits.
plain: And if we can attack a smaller force with a larger one in this way, our opponents will be in serious trouble.
notes: 'Dire straits' means serious trouble.

original: The spot where we intend to fight must not be made known; for then the enemy will have to prepare against a possible attack at several different points; and his forces being thus distributed in many directions, the numbers we shall have to face at any given point will be proportionately few.
plain: Where we intend to fight must not be made known. Then the enemy will have to prepare for attack at several different points, and with his forces spread in many directions, the numbers we face at any one point will be correspondingly small.

original: For should the enemy strengthen his van, he will weaken his rear; should he strengthen his rear, he will weaken his van; should he strengthen his left, he will weaken his right; should he strengthen his right, he will weaken his left. If he sends reinforcements everywhere, he will everywhere be weak.
plain: If the enemy strengthens his front, he weakens his rear; if he strengthens his rear, he weakens his front. If he strengthens his left, he weakens his right; if he strengthens his right, he weakens his left. If he sends reinforcements everywhere, he will be weak everywhere.
notes: 'Van' means the front of an army.

original: Numerical weakness comes from having to prepare against possible attacks; numerical strength, from compelling our adversary to make these preparations against us.
plain: Being outnumbered comes from having to prepare against possible attacks. Having the greater numbers comes from forcing the enemy to make those preparations against us.
notes: 'Numerical weakness' means being outnumbered at the point of contact.

original: Knowing the place and the time of the coming battle, we may concentrate from the greatest distances in order to fight.
plain: If we know where and when the battle will be, we can bring our forces together from the greatest distances to fight.

original: But if neither time nor place be known, then the left wing will be impotent to succour the right, the right equally impotent to succour the left, the van unable to relieve the rear, or the rear to support the van. How much more so if the furthest portions of the army are anything under a hundred li apart, and even the nearest are separated by several li!
plain: But if neither time nor place is known, the left wing cannot help the right, the right cannot help the left, the front cannot relieve the rear, and the rear cannot support the front. How much worse when the farthest parts of the army are up to a hundred li apart, and even the nearest are several li apart!
notes: 'Succour' means help. 'Impotent' means powerless. 'Li' is a distance of a few hundred metres (see II.1). 'Anything under a hundred li' is Giles's phrasing for 'as much as a hundred li'.

original: Though according to my estimate the soldiers of Yüeh exceed our own in number, that shall advantage them nothing in the matter of victory. I say then that victory can be achieved.
plain: Though by my estimate the soldiers of Yüeh outnumber ours, that will not help them win. So I say victory can be achieved.
notes: Yüeh (Yue) was a rival state of Wu, the state Sun Tzu is traditionally said to have served. This is one of the few points tied to a specific historical setting.

original: Though the enemy be stronger in numbers, we may prevent him from fighting. Scheme so as to discover his plans and the likelihood of their success.
plain: Even if the enemy has more troops, we can stop him from fighting. Plan so as to find out his plans and how likely they are to succeed.
notes: 'Scheme' here means plan, without a negative sense.

original: Rouse him, and learn the principle of his activity or inactivity. Force him to reveal himself, so as to find out his vulnerable spots.
plain: Stir him up, and learn what makes him move or stay still. Force him to show himself, so as to find his weak spots.
notes: 'The principle of his activity or inactivity' is Giles's phrase. The Chinese may also mean 'his pattern of movement'. Some versions read the second sentence as 'find out where the ground is deadly or safe for him'.

original: Carefully compare the opposing army with your own, so that you may know where strength is superabundant and where it is deficient.
plain: Compare the opposing army with your own carefully, so you know where you have more strength than you need and where you have too little.

original: In making tactical dispositions, the highest pitch you can attain is to conceal them; conceal your dispositions, and you will be safe from the prying of the subtlest spies, from the machinations of the wisest brains.
plain: The highest skill in positioning your forces is to hide that positioning. Hide your dispositions and you will be safe from the most skilled spies and the cleverest minds.
notes: The Chinese speaks of making one's dispositions 'formless'. 'Machinations' means scheming.

original: How victory may be produced for them out of the enemy’s own tactics—that is what the multitude cannot comprehend.
plain: How victory can be created for them out of the enemy's own tactics - that is what ordinary people cannot understand.
notes: 'For them' is unclear in Giles - it probably means 'for the troops' or 'for the many'. Left open.

original: All men can see the tactics whereby I conquer, but what none can see is the strategy out of which victory is evolved.
plain: Everyone can see the tactics by which I win, but no one can see the strategy from which the victory grows.
notes: Giles uses 'tactics' and 'strategy' in their modern sense here; the Chinese contrasts the visible form with what produced it.

original: Do not repeat the tactics which have gained you one victory, but let your methods be regulated by the infinite variety of circumstances.
plain: Do not repeat the tactics that won you a victory. Let your methods be shaped by the endless variety of circumstances.

original: Military tactics are like unto water; for water in its natural course runs away from high places and hastens downwards.
plain: Military tactics are like water: water naturally runs away from high places and hurries downwards.
notes: 'Like unto' is old phrasing for 'like'.

original: So in war, the way is to avoid what is strong and to strike at what is weak.
plain: So in war, the way is to avoid what is strong and strike at what is weak.
notes: 'Strong' and 'weak' also render 'full' and 'empty' (see V.4).

original: Water shapes its course according to the nature of the ground over which it flows; the soldier works out his victory in relation to the foe whom he is facing.
plain: Water shapes its course to the ground it flows over; the soldier works out his victory in relation to the enemy he faces.

original: Therefore, just as water retains no constant shape, so in warfare there are no constant conditions.
plain: So just as water keeps no fixed shape, in war there are no fixed conditions.

original: He who can modify his tactics in relation to his opponent and thereby succeed in winning, may be called a heaven-born captain.
plain: Someone who can change his tactics in response to his opponent and win by doing so can be called a heaven-born commander.
notes: 'Heaven-born captain' is Giles's phrase; other translators render it 'divine' or 'spirit-like'.

original: The five elements (water, fire, wood, metal, earth) are not always equally predominant; the four seasons make way for each other in turn. There are short days and long; the moon has its periods of waning and waxing.
plain: The five elements (water, fire, wood, metal and earth) do not always dominate equally; the four seasons give way to each other in turn. There are short days and long ones; the moon waxes and wanes.
notes: The 'five elements' (wuxing) are phases of a traditional Chinese cycle in which each overcomes another; none stays on top. 'Waning and waxing' means shrinking and growing.

original: Sun Tzŭ said: In war, the general receives his commands from the sovereign.
plain: Sun Tzu said: In war, the general receives his orders from the ruler.
notes: 'Sovereign' means the ruler.

original: Having collected an army and concentrated his forces, he must blend and harmonise the different elements thereof before pitching his camp.
plain: Having raised an army and brought his forces together, he must blend and harmonise its different parts before setting up camp.
notes: The Chinese is often read as 'he faces the enemy and camps', and 'blend and harmonise' is Giles's gloss. The second half may describe positioning against the enemy rather than internal harmony.

original: After that, comes tactical manœuvering, than which there is nothing more difficult. The difficulty of tactical manœuvering consists in turning the devious into the direct, and misfortune into gain.
plain: After that comes manoeuvring, and nothing is harder. The difficulty is turning the roundabout into the direct, and bad fortune into gain.
notes: 'Devious' here means roundabout or indirect, not dishonest.

original: Thus, to take a long and circuitous route, after enticing the enemy out of the way, and though starting after him, to contrive to reach the goal before him, shows knowledge of the artifice of deviation.
plain: So taking a long, roundabout route after luring the enemy out of the way, and reaching the goal before him despite setting out after him, shows you understand the trick of deviation.
notes: 'Artifice of deviation' means the skill of the indirect route - making the long way the quick way.

original: Manœuvering with an army is advantageous; with an undisciplined multitude, most dangerous.
plain: Manoeuvring with a disciplined army brings advantage; with an undisciplined crowd it is very dangerous.
notes: Giles's reading. Many translators read it differently: manoeuvring can bring advantage, and manoeuvring can bring danger. The rewrite keeps Giles.

original: If you set a fully equipped army in march in order to snatch an advantage, the chances are that you will be too late. On the other hand, to detach a flying column for the purpose involves the sacrifice of its baggage and stores.
plain: If you march a fully equipped army to grab an advantage, you will probably be too late. On the other hand, sending a fast detachment ahead means giving up its baggage and supplies.
notes: 'Flying column' means a fast-moving detachment travelling light.

original: Thus, if you order your men to roll up their buff-coats, and make forced marches without halting day or night, covering double the usual distance at a stretch, doing a hundred li in order to wrest an advantage, the leaders of all your three divisions will fall into the hands of the enemy.
plain: So if you order your men to roll up their coats and make forced marches day and night, covering twice the usual distance in one go, marching a hundred li to seize an advantage, the leaders of all three divisions will fall into enemy hands.
notes: 'Buff-coats' are leather jackets - here, the soldiers' armour or kit. 'Li' see II.1. An army was often divided into three divisions.

original: The stronger men will be in front, the jaded ones will fall behind, and on this plan only one-tenth of your army will reach its destination.
plain: The stronger men will be out in front, the tired ones will fall behind, and by this plan only a tenth of your army will arrive.
notes: 'Jaded' means worn out.

original: If you march fifty li in order to outmanœuver the enemy, you will lose the leader of your first division, and only half your force will reach the goal.
plain: If you march fifty li to outmanoeuvre the enemy, you will lose the leader of your first division, and only half your force will arrive.

original: If you march thirty li with the same object, two-thirds of your army will arrive.
plain: If you march thirty li for the same purpose, two-thirds of your army will arrive.

original: We may take it then that an army without its baggage-train is lost; without provisions it is lost; without bases of supply it is lost.
plain: So we can take it that an army without its baggage train is lost; without provisions it is lost; without supply bases it is lost.

original: We cannot enter into alliances until we are acquainted with the designs of our neighbours.
plain: We cannot form alliances until we know what our neighbours intend.
notes: This point and the next two are repeated almost word for word in XI.52.

original: We are not fit to lead an army on the march unless we are familiar with the face of the country—its mountains and forests, its pitfalls and precipices, its marshes and swamps.
plain: We are not fit to lead an army on the march unless we know the lie of the land - its mountains and forests, its traps and cliffs, its marshes and swamps.
notes: 'The face of the country' means the terrain. 'Pitfalls' means hidden hazards.

original: We shall be unable to turn natural advantages to account unless we make use of local guides.
plain: We cannot turn natural advantages to our benefit unless we use local guides.

original: In war, practise dissimulation, and you will succeed. Move only if there is a real advantage to be gained.
plain: In war, practise deception and you will succeed. Move only if there is a real advantage to be gained.
notes: 'Dissimulation' means hiding your true intentions or putting on a false appearance.

original: Whether to concentrate or to divide your troops, must be decided by circumstances.
plain: Whether to concentrate or split your troops must depend on circumstances.

original: Let your rapidity be that of the wind, your compactness that of the forest.
plain: Be as fast as the wind and as tight-knit as the forest.
notes: 'Compactness' may also be read as calm or stately order, like a forest.

original: In raiding and plundering be like fire, in immovability like a mountain.
plain: In raiding and plundering, be like fire; in holding still, be like a mountain.
notes: 'Immovability' means steadiness - refusing to be moved.

original: Let your plans be dark and impenetrable as night, and when you move, fall like a thunderbolt.
plain: Let your plans be as dark and hard to see into as night, and when you move, strike like a thunderbolt.

original: When you plunder a countryside, let the spoil be divided amongst your men; when you capture new territory, cut it up into allotments for the benefit of the soldiery.
plain: When you plunder a district, share the spoils among your men. When you capture new territory, divide it into plots for the benefit of the soldiers.
notes: Some translators read this as dividing your forces to collect plunder and to hold new ground, rather than rewarding the soldiers. Kept to Giles.

original: Ponder and deliberate before you make a move.
plain: Think it over carefully before you make a move.
notes: Often rendered 'weigh the situation before you move' - with an image of balancing scales.

original: He will conquer who has learnt the artifice of deviation. Such is the art of manœuvering.
plain: Whoever has learned the trick of deviation will win. That is the art of manoeuvring.
notes: See VII.4 on deviation.

original: The Book of Army Management says: On the field of battle, the spoken word does not carry far enough: hence the institution of gongs and drums. Nor can ordinary objects be seen clearly enough: hence the institution of banners and flags.
plain: The Book of Army Management says: On the battlefield the spoken word does not carry far enough, so gongs and drums were introduced. Ordinary objects cannot be seen clearly enough, so banners and flags were introduced.
notes: 'The Book of Army Management' is an older military text Sun Tzu is quoting; it has not survived.

original: Gongs and drums, banners and flags, are means whereby the ears and eyes of the host may be focussed on one particular point.
plain: Gongs and drums, banners and flags are the means of focusing the ears and eyes of the whole army on one point.
notes: 'Host' means army.

original: The host thus forming a single united body, is it impossible either for the brave to advance alone, or for the cowardly to retreat alone. This is the art of handling large masses of men.
plain: With the army formed into one united body like this, the brave cannot advance alone and the cowardly cannot retreat alone. This is the art of handling large numbers of men.
notes: Giles's text has 'is it impossible' (a word-order slip for 'it is impossible'); the original is kept exactly.

original: In night-fighting, then, make much use of signal-fires and drums, and in fighting by day, of flags and banners, as a means of influencing the ears and eyes of your army.
plain: So in night fighting, make heavy use of signal fires and drums, and in daytime fighting, of flags and banners, to steer the ears and eyes of your army.
notes: Some translators read the last part as aimed at the enemy's eyes and ears - to confuse them - rather than your own army's. Giles chooses your own army.

original: A whole army may be robbed of its spirit; a commander-in-chief may be robbed of his presence of mind.
plain: A whole army can be robbed of its spirit; a commander-in-chief can be robbed of his composure.
notes: 'Presence of mind' means calm, clear judgement under pressure.

original: Now a soldier’s spirit is keenest in the morning; by noonday it has begun to flag; and in the evening, his mind is bent only on returning to camp.
plain: A soldier's spirit is strongest in the morning; by midday it has begun to fade; and by evening his mind is only on getting back to camp.
notes: Some translators read 'morning, noon, evening' as the early, middle and late stages of a campaign or battle rather than times of day. Giles takes them as times of day.

original: A clever general, therefore, avoids an army when its spirit is keen, but attacks it when it is sluggish and inclined to return. This is the art of studying moods.
plain: So a clever general avoids an army when its spirit is high and attacks it when it is sluggish and wanting to go back. This is the art of reading moods.
notes: 'Studying moods' means managing morale - your own and the enemy's.

original: Disciplined and calm, to await the appearance of disorder and hubbub amongst the enemy:—this is the art of retaining self-possession.
plain: Disciplined and calm, waiting for disorder and uproar to appear among the enemy: this is the art of keeping your composure.
notes: 'Hubbub' means noisy confusion.

original: To be near the goal while the enemy is still far from it, to wait at ease while the enemy is toiling and struggling, to be well-fed while the enemy is famished:—this is the art of husbanding one’s strength.
plain: Being near the goal while the enemy is still far from it, waiting at ease while the enemy toils and struggles, being well fed while the enemy is starving: this is the art of conserving your strength.
notes: 'Husbanding' means using carefully, conserving.

original: To refrain from intercepting an enemy whose banners are in perfect order, to refrain from attacking an army drawn up in calm and confident array:—this is the art of studying circumstances.
plain: Holding back from intercepting an enemy whose banners are in perfect order, and from attacking an army drawn up calmly and confidently: this is the art of reading circumstances.

original: It is a military axiom not to advance uphill against the enemy, nor to oppose him when he comes downhill.
plain: It is a military rule not to attack uphill against the enemy, nor to confront him when he is coming downhill.
notes: 'Axiom' means a basic rule.

original: Do not pursue an enemy who simulates flight; do not attack soldiers whose temper is keen.
plain: Do not chase an enemy who is pretending to flee. Do not attack soldiers whose spirits are high.
notes: 'Temper' means spirit or mood here, not anger.

original: Do not swallow a bait offered by the enemy. Do not interfere with an army that is returning home.
plain: Do not take a bait the enemy offers. Do not get in the way of an army heading home.

original: When you surround an army, leave an outlet free. Do not press a desperate foe too hard.
plain: When you surround an army, leave a way out open. Do not push a desperate enemy too hard.
notes: Whether the 'outlet' is mercy or a tactic to stop the enemy fighting to the death is not stated here; compare XI.23-24.

original: Such is the art of warfare.
plain: That is the art of warfare.

original: Sun Tzŭ said: In war, the general receives his commands from the sovereign, collects his army and concentrates his forces.
plain: Sun Tzu said: In war, the general receives his orders from the ruler, raises his army and brings his forces together.
notes: This repeats the opening of VII.1-2 almost word for word, which may be a copying error in the old text.

original: When in difficult country, do not encamp. In country where high roads intersect, join hands with your allies. Do not linger in dangerously isolated positions. In hemmed-in situations, you must resort to stratagem. In a desperate position, you must fight.
plain: In difficult country, do not camp. Where main roads cross, join up with your allies. Do not stay in dangerously cut-off positions. When hemmed in, you must use stratagems. When in a desperate position, you must fight.
notes: These are short versions of rules for kinds of ground set out fully in XI.11-14. 'Hemmed-in' means surrounded or closed off.

original: There are roads which must not be followed, armies which must be not attacked, towns which must not be besieged, positions which must not be contested, commands of the sovereign which must not be obeyed.
plain: There are roads that must not be taken, armies that must not be attacked, towns that must not be besieged, positions that must not be fought over, and orders from the ruler that must not be obeyed.
notes: Giles's text has 'must be not attacked' (word-order slip); the original is kept exactly. The last clause is bold - it sets limits on a ruler's authority over the general.

original: The general who thoroughly understands the advantages that accompany variation of tactics knows how to handle his troops.
plain: A general who fully understands the advantages of varying his tactics knows how to handle his troops.

original: The general who does not understand these, may be well acquainted with the configuration of the country, yet he will not be able to turn his knowledge to practical account.
plain: A general who does not understand them may know the lie of the land well, yet he will not be able to put that knowledge to practical use.
notes: 'Configuration of the country' means the shape of the terrain.

original: So, the student of war who is unversed in the art of war of varying his plans, even though he be acquainted with the Five Advantages, will fail to make the best use of his men.
plain: So a student of war who has not learned how to vary his plans will fail to make the best use of his men, even if he knows the Five Advantages.
notes: 'The Five Advantages' is unclear. Giles's commentary links it to the five situations in VIII.2 (or to the five 'do nots' in VIII.3). The text itself does not say. The phrase 'unversed in the art of war of varying his plans' is Giles's clumsy wording for 'not skilled at varying his plans'.

original: Hence in the wise leader’s plans, considerations of advantage and of disadvantage will be blended together.
plain: So a wise leader's plans weigh advantages and disadvantages together.

original: If our expectation of advantage be tempered in this way, we may succeed in accomplishing the essential part of our schemes.
plain: If our hopes of advantage are balanced in this way, we can succeed in the main part of our plans.
notes: 'Tempered' means moderated or balanced.

original: If, on the other hand, in the midst of difficulties we are always ready to seize an advantage, we may extricate ourselves from misfortune.
plain: If, on the other hand, we stay ready to seize an advantage even in the middle of difficulties, we can get ourselves out of trouble.
notes: 'Extricate' means free or get out.

original: Reduce the hostile chiefs by inflicting damage on them; and make trouble for them, and keep them constantly engaged; hold out specious allurements, and make them rush to any given point.
plain: Wear down hostile leaders by doing them damage; make trouble for them and keep them constantly busy; offer them tempting lures and make them rush to wherever you choose.
notes: 'Specious allurements' means attractive but deceptive offers.

original: The art of war teaches us to rely not on the likelihood of the enemy’s not coming, but on our own readiness to receive him; not on the chance of his not attacking, but rather on the fact that we have made our position unassailable.
plain: The art of war teaches us not to count on the enemy not coming, but on our own readiness to meet him; not on the chance that he will not attack, but on having made our position impossible to attack.
notes: 'Unassailable' means impossible to attack successfully.

Translators differ on (2) and (5). (2) is also rendered 'too much concern for staying alive'. (5) is also rendered 'too much love for the people' - which may mean civilians, not only soldiers. 'Over-solicitude' means excessive concern.

original: These are the five besetting sins of a general, ruinous to the conduct of war.
plain: These are the five habitual failings of a general, and they ruin the conduct of war.
notes: 'Besetting sins' means persistent faults.

original: When an army is overthrown and its leader slain, the cause will surely be found among these five dangerous faults. Let them be a subject of meditation.
plain: When an army is overthrown and its leader killed, the cause will surely be found among these five dangerous faults. Think about them carefully.
notes: 'Let them be a subject of meditation' means reflect on them, not a religious practice.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: Sun Tzŭ said: We come now to the question of encamping the army, and observing signs of the enemy. Pass quickly over mountains, and keep in the neighbourhood of valleys.
plain: Sun Tzu said: We now come to camping the army and watching for signs of the enemy. Cross mountains quickly, and keep close to valleys.
notes: 'Keep in the neighbourhood of valleys' likely means stay near valleys for water and grazing.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: Camp in high places, facing the sun. Do not climb heights in order to fight. So much for mountain warfare.
plain: Camp on high ground facing the sun. Do not climb heights to fight. That is all on fighting in mountains.
notes: 'Facing the sun' generally means facing south, the sunny side in the northern hemisphere. Some read 'do not climb heights to fight' as 'do not attack an enemy on higher ground'.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: After crossing a river, you should get far away from it.
plain: After crossing a river, get well away from it.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: When an invading force crosses a river in its onward march, do not advance to meet it in mid-stream. It will be best to let half the army get across, and then deliver your attack.
plain: When an invading force crosses a river as it advances, do not go to meet it midstream. It is best to let half the army get across, then attack.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: If you are anxious to fight, you should not go to meet the invader near a river which he has to cross.
plain: If you want to fight, do not go to meet the invader close to a river he has to cross.
notes: The reason is not given in the text. Read with IX.4, the point seems to be letting him cross rather than blocking him at the bank.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: Moor your craft higher up than the enemy, and facing the sun. Do not move up-stream to meet the enemy. So much for river warfare.
plain: Moor your boats upstream of the enemy and facing the sun. Do not move upstream to meet the enemy. That is all on fighting by rivers.
notes: 'Craft' means boats. 'Facing the sun' see IX.2. Some read 'moor your craft higher up' as 'camp on high ground'.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: In crossing salt-marshes, your sole concern should be to get over them quickly, without any delay.
plain: When crossing salt marshes, your only concern should be to get across them quickly, without any delay.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: If forced to fight in a salt-marsh, you should have water and grass near you, and get your back to a clump of trees. So much for operations in salt-marshes.
plain: If you are forced to fight in a salt marsh, keep water and grass near you and get your back to a clump of trees. That is all on fighting in salt marshes.
notes: Water and grass are presumably for men and horses; the text does not explain the trees.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: In dry, level country, take up an easily accessible position with rising ground to your right and on your rear, so that the danger may be in front, and safety lie behind. So much for campaigning in flat country.
plain: In dry, flat country, take a position that is easy to reach, with rising ground on your right and behind you, so that danger lies ahead and safety behind. That is all on fighting in flat country.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: These are the four useful branches of military knowledge which enabled the Yellow Emperor to vanquish four several sovereigns.
plain: These are the four useful branches of military knowledge that let the Yellow Emperor defeat four other rulers.
notes: The Yellow Emperor (Huangdi) is a legendary founding ruler of Chinese civilisation. 'Four several sovereigns' means four separate rulers. The 'four branches' are the mountain, river, marsh and flat-country rules above.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: All armies prefer high ground to low, and sunny places to dark.
plain: All armies prefer high ground to low, and sunny places to dark ones.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: If you are careful of your men, and camp on hard ground, the army will be free from disease of every kind, and this will spell victory.
