plain: If you look after your men and camp on firm ground, the army will be free of every kind of disease, and this will mean victory.
notes: 'Spell victory' means lead to victory.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: When you come to a hill or a bank, occupy the sunny side, with the slope on your right rear. Thus you will at once act for the benefit of your soldiers and utilise the natural advantages of the ground.
plain: When you reach a hill or a bank, take the sunny side, with the slope behind you on your right. That way you both benefit your soldiers and use the natural advantages of the ground.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: When, in consequence of heavy rains up-country, a river which you wish to ford is swollen and flecked with foam, you must wait until it subsides.
plain: When heavy rain upstream has made a river you want to cross swollen and foaming, you must wait until it goes down.
notes: 'Ford' means cross on foot.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: Country in which there are precipitous cliffs with torrents running between, deep natural hollows, confined places, tangled thickets, quagmires and crevasses, should be left with all possible speed and not approached.
plain: Country with steep cliffs and torrents between them, deep natural hollows, enclosed places, tangled thickets, bogs and crevices should be left as fast as possible and not approached.
notes: Each feature has a specific name in the Chinese (for example 'Heaven's Well', 'Heaven's Prison'); Giles describes them rather than translating the names.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: While we keep away from such places, we should get the enemy to approach them; while we face them, we should let the enemy have them on his rear.
plain: While we keep away from such places, we should get the enemy to approach them; while we face them, we should let the enemy have them at his back.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: If in the neighbourhood of your camp there should be any hilly country, ponds surrounded by aquatic grass, hollow basins filled with reeds, or woods with thick undergrowth, they must be carefully routed out and searched; for these are places where men in ambush or insidious spies are likely to be lurking.
plain: If near your camp there is any hilly country, ponds surrounded by water grass, hollows full of reeds, or woods with thick undergrowth, they must be thoroughly searched, because these are places where men in ambush or sneaky spies are likely to be hiding.
notes: 'Insidious' means sly or treacherous. Some versions read 'hilly country' as 'narrow passes'.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: When the enemy is close at hand and remains quiet, he is relying on the natural strength of his position.
plain: When the enemy is close by and stays quiet, he is relying on the natural strength of his position.
notes: IX.18-39 is a list of signs to read. Many are tied to ancient conditions.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: When he keeps aloof and tries to provoke a battle, he is anxious for the other side to advance.
plain: When he stays at a distance and tries to provoke a battle, he wants the other side to advance.
notes: 'Aloof' means at a distance.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: If his place of encampment is easy of access, he is tendering a bait.
plain: If his camp is easy to get to, he is offering a bait.
notes: 'Tendering' means offering.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: Movement amongst the trees of a forest shows that the enemy is advancing. The appearance of a number of screens in the midst of thick grass means that the enemy wants to make us suspicious.
plain: Movement among the trees of a forest shows the enemy is advancing. A number of screens set up in thick grass means the enemy wants to make us suspicious.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: The rising of birds in their flight is the sign of an ambuscade. Startled beasts indicate that a sudden attack is coming.
plain: Birds rising in flight are a sign of an ambush. Startled animals mean a sudden attack is coming.
notes: 'Ambuscade' means ambush.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: When there is dust rising in a high column, it is the sign of chariots advancing; when the dust is low, but spread over a wide area, it betokens the approach of infantry. When it branches out in different directions, it shows that parties have been sent to collect firewood. A few clouds of dust moving to and fro signify that the army is encamping.
plain: Dust rising in a high column is a sign of chariots advancing; dust low but spread over a wide area means infantry approaching. Dust branching off in different directions shows that parties have been sent to collect firewood. A few clouds of dust moving back and forth mean the army is setting up camp.
notes: 'Betokens' means signals.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: Humble words and increased preparations are signs that the enemy is about to advance. Violent language and driving forward as if to the attack are signs that he will retreat.
plain: Humble words with increased preparations are signs the enemy is about to advance. Aggressive language and pushing forward as if to attack are signs that he will retreat.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: When the light chariots come out first and take up a position on the wings, it is a sign that the enemy is forming for battle.
plain: When light chariots come out first and take up position on the flanks, the enemy is forming up for battle.
notes: 'Wings' means flanks - the sides of the army.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: Peace proposals unaccompanied by a sworn covenant indicate a plot.
plain: Peace offers that come without a sworn agreement mean a plot.
notes: 'Covenant' means a binding agreement. Some translators read this as 'peace offers made without prior negotiation' or 'when not under pressure'.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: When there is much running about and the soldiers fall into rank, it means that the critical moment has come.
plain: When there is a lot of running about and the soldiers fall into line, the critical moment has come.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: When some are seen advancing and some retreating, it is a lure.
plain: When some are seen advancing and some retreating, it is a lure.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: When the soldiers stand leaning on their spears, they are faint from want of food.
plain: When the soldiers stand leaning on their spears, they are faint with hunger.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: If those who are sent to draw water begin by drinking themselves, the army is suffering from thirst.
plain: If those sent to fetch water start by drinking it themselves, the army is suffering from thirst.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: If the enemy sees an advantage to be gained and makes no effort to secure it, the soldiers are exhausted.
plain: If the enemy sees an advantage to be gained and makes no attempt to take it, the soldiers are exhausted.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: If birds gather on any spot, it is unoccupied. Clamour by night betokens nervousness.
plain: If birds gather on a spot, it is empty. Noise at night means nervousness.
notes: 'Clamour' means loud noise.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: If there is disturbance in the camp, the general’s authority is weak. If the banners and flags are shifted about, sedition is afoot. If the officers are angry, it means that the men are weary.
plain: If there is disturbance in the camp, the general's authority is weak. If banners and flags are being moved about, rebellion is brewing. If the officers are angry, the men are tired.
notes: 'Sedition' means rebellion or incitement against authority. 'Afoot' means under way.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: When an army feeds its horses with grain and kills its cattle for food, and when the men do not hang their cooking-pots over the camp-fires, showing that they will not return to their tents, you may know that they are determined to fight to the death.
plain: When an army feeds its horses grain and kills its cattle for food, and the men do not hang their cooking pots over the campfires - showing they will not go back to their tents - you can know they are determined to fight to the death.
notes: Feeding grain to horses and killing cattle uses up supplies kept for the long term - a sign they expect no future.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: The sight of men whispering together in small knots or speaking in subdued tones points to disaffection amongst the rank and file.
plain: Men whispering together in small groups or speaking in low voices point to discontent among the ordinary soldiers.
notes: 'Disaffection' means discontent or loss of loyalty. 'Rank and file' means ordinary soldiers.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: Too frequent rewards signify that the enemy is at the end of his resources; too many punishments betray a condition of dire distress.
plain: Too-frequent rewards show the enemy is at the end of his resources; too many punishments reveal serious distress.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: To begin by bluster, but afterwards to take fright at the enemy’s numbers, shows a supreme lack of intelligence.
plain: Starting with bluster but then taking fright at the enemy's numbers shows a total lack of intelligence.
notes: Unclear whose behaviour this is. It may describe an enemy general (a sign to read) or warn against your own conduct. Some translators read it as a general who is harsh at first then fearful of his own men.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: When envoys are sent with compliments in their mouths, it is a sign that the enemy wishes for a truce.
plain: When envoys arrive full of compliments, the enemy wants a truce.
notes: Some read it as wanting 'a pause' or 'time to rest' rather than a formal truce.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: If the enemy’s troops march up angrily and remain facing ours for a long time without either joining battle or taking themselves off again, the situation is one that demands great vigilance and circumspection.
plain: If the enemy's troops march up angrily and stay facing ours for a long time without either fighting or leaving, the situation needs great watchfulness and caution.
notes: 'Circumspection' means caution.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: If our troops are no more in number than the enemy, that is amply sufficient; it only means that no direct attack can be made. What we can do is simply to concentrate all our available strength, keep a close watch on the enemy, and obtain reinforcements.
plain: If our troops are no more numerous than the enemy, that is quite enough; it only means we cannot make a direct attack. What we can do is concentrate all our available strength, keep a close watch on the enemy, and get reinforcements.
notes: The last clause is disputed. Giles has 'obtain reinforcements'; other translators read it as 'win over your men' or 'take the enemy' - the Chinese can mean gaining people in several senses.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: He who exercises no forethought but makes light of his opponents is sure to be captured by them.
plain: Whoever does not think ahead and underestimates his opponents is sure to be captured by them.
notes: 'Makes light of' means underestimates.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: If soldiers are punished before they have grown attached to you, they will not prove submissive; and, unless submissive, then will be practically useless. If, when the soldiers have become attached to you, punishments are not enforced, they will still be useless.
plain: If soldiers are punished before they have grown attached to you, they will not be obedient - and if not obedient, they will be practically useless. If, once they are attached to you, punishments are not enforced, they will still be useless.
notes: 'Submissive' means obedient. Giles's 'then will be practically useless' is missing 'they'; kept exactly in the original.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: Therefore soldiers must be treated in the first instance with humanity, but kept under control by means of iron discipline. This is a certain road to victory.
plain: So soldiers must first be treated with humanity, but kept in line by strict discipline. This is a sure road to victory.
notes: The Chinese pair is often rendered 'civil' and 'martial' (wen and wu) - command them with culture and kindness, unify them with military discipline. 'Iron discipline' is Giles's phrase.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: If in training soldiers commands are habitually enforced, the army will be well-disciplined; if not, its discipline will be bad.
plain: If orders are consistently enforced while training soldiers, the army will be well disciplined; if not, its discipline will be poor.

chapter: IX. The Army on the March
original: If a general shows confidence in his men but always insists on his orders being obeyed, the gain will be mutual.
plain: If a general shows trust in his men but always insists on his orders being obeyed, both sides gain.
notes: Variant readings: some texts read it as 'if orders are consistently trustworthy, the general and the troops will get on'. Giles's 'the gain will be mutual' is open about what is gained.

original: Sun Tzŭ said: We may distinguish six kinds of terrain, to wit: (1) Accessible ground; (2) entangling ground; (3) temporising ground; (4) narrow passes; (5) precipitous heights; (6) positions at a great distance from the enemy.
plain: Sun Tzu said: We can distinguish six kinds of terrain: (1) accessible ground; (2) entangling ground; (3) stalemate ground; (4) narrow passes; (5) steep heights; (6) positions a long way from the enemy.
notes: 'To wit' means namely. 'Temporising' means holding back or playing for time; the rewrite uses 'stalemate', which X.6 defines. The six names are Giles's; other versions use 'open', 'hanging', 'deadlock' and so on.

original: Ground which can be freely traversed by both sides is called accessible.
plain: Ground both sides can move across freely is called accessible.

original: With regard to ground of this nature, be before the enemy in occupying the raised and sunny spots, and carefully guard your line of supplies. Then you will be able to fight with advantage.
plain: On this kind of ground, get to the high, sunny spots before the enemy and guard your supply line carefully. Then you can fight with the advantage.

original: Ground which can be abandoned but is hard to re-occupy is called entangling.
plain: Ground you can leave but find hard to get back onto is called entangling.

original: From a position of this sort, if the enemy is unprepared, you may sally forth and defeat him. But if the enemy is prepared for your coming, and you fail to defeat him, then, return being impossible, disaster will ensue.
plain: From a position like this, if the enemy is unprepared, you can come out and defeat him. But if the enemy is ready for you and you fail to defeat him, then, since you cannot get back, disaster will follow.
notes: 'Sally forth' means rush out to attack.

original: When the position is such that neither side will gain by making the first move, it is called temporising ground.
plain: When the position is such that neither side gains by moving first, it is called stalemate ground.
notes: Giles's 'temporising' - see X.1.

original: In a position of this sort, even though the enemy should offer us an attractive bait, it will be advisable not to stir forth, but rather to retreat, thus enticing the enemy in his turn; then, when part of his army has come out, we may deliver our attack with advantage.
plain: In a position like this, even if the enemy offers us a tempting bait, it is better not to come out but to withdraw, luring the enemy in turn. Then, when part of his army has come out, we can attack with the advantage.

original: With regard to narrow passes, if you can occupy them first, let them be strongly garrisoned and await the advent of the enemy.
plain: With narrow passes, if you can occupy them first, garrison them strongly and wait for the enemy to arrive.
notes: 'Garrisoned' means manned with troops. 'Advent' means arrival.

original: Should the enemy forestall you in occupying a pass, do not go after him if the pass is fully garrisoned, but only if it is weakly garrisoned.
plain: If the enemy gets to a pass before you, do not go after him if it is fully manned - only if it is weakly manned.
notes: 'Forestall' means get in first.

original: With regard to precipitous heights, if you are beforehand with your adversary, you should occupy the raised and sunny spots, and there wait for him to come up.
plain: With steep heights, if you get there before your opponent, occupy the high, sunny spots and wait there for him to come up.
notes: 'Beforehand with' means ahead of.

original: If the enemy has occupied them before you, do not follow him, but retreat and try to entice him away.
plain: If the enemy has occupied them before you, do not follow him up; withdraw and try to lure him away.

original: If you are situated at a great distance from the enemy, and the strength of the two armies is equal, it is not easy to provoke a battle, and fighting will be to your disadvantage.
plain: If you are a long way from the enemy and the two armies are equally strong, it is hard to start a battle, and fighting will be to your disadvantage.

original: These six are the principles connected with Earth. The general who has attained a responsible post must be careful to study them.
plain: These six are the principles to do with Earth. A general who holds a responsible post must study them carefully.
notes: 'Earth' is the terrain factor from I.8.

original: Now an army is exposed to six several calamities, not arising from natural causes, but from faults for which the general is responsible. These are: (1) Flight; (2) insubordination; (3) collapse; (4) ruin; (5) disorganisation; (6) rout.
plain: An army is open to six kinds of disaster that do not come from natural causes but from faults the general is responsible for. They are: (1) flight; (2) insubordination; (3) collapse; (4) ruin; (5) disorganisation; (6) rout.
notes: 'Six several calamities' means six separate disasters. 'Insubordination' means disobedience. 'Rout' means a disorderly defeat and flight.

original: Other conditions being equal, if one force is hurled against another ten times its size, the result will be the flight of the former.
plain: Other things being equal, if one force is thrown against another ten times its size, the result will be the flight of the smaller.
notes: Giles italicised each disaster's name in X.15-19; the markers are removed.

original: When the common soldiers are too strong and their officers too weak, the result is insubordination. When the officers are too strong and the common soldiers too weak, the result is collapse.
plain: When the ordinary soldiers are too strong and their officers too weak, the result is insubordination. When the officers are too strong and the ordinary soldiers too weak, the result is collapse.

original: When the higher officers are angry and insubordinate, and on meeting the enemy give battle on their own account from a feeling of resentment, before the commander-in-chief can tell whether or no he is in a position to fight, the result is ruin.
plain: When senior officers are angry and disobedient, and on meeting the enemy start fighting on their own out of resentment before the commander-in-chief can judge whether he is in a position to fight, the result is ruin.
notes: 'Whether or no' is old phrasing for 'whether or not'.

original: When the general is weak and without authority; when his orders are not clear and distinct; when there are no fixed duties assigned to officers and men, and the ranks are formed in a slovenly haphazard manner, the result is utter disorganisation.
plain: When the general is weak and lacks authority, when his orders are not clear and precise, when officers and men have no fixed duties, and the ranks are formed in a sloppy, haphazard way, the result is complete disorganisation.
notes: 'Slovenly' means careless or sloppy.

original: When a general, unable to estimate the enemy’s strength, allows an inferior force to engage a larger one, or hurls a weak detachment against a powerful one, and neglects to place picked soldiers in the front rank, the result must be a rout.
plain: When a general who cannot judge the enemy's strength lets a smaller force engage a larger one, or throws a weak detachment against a powerful one, and fails to put picked soldiers in the front line, the result must be a rout.
notes: 'Picked soldiers' means elite, selected troops.

original: These are six ways of courting defeat, which must be carefully noted by the general who has attained a responsible post.
plain: These are six ways of inviting defeat, which a general in a responsible post must take careful note of.
notes: 'Courting defeat' means inviting it.

original: The natural formation of the country is the soldier’s best ally; but a power of estimating the adversary, of controlling the forces of victory, and of shrewdly calculating difficulties, dangers and distances, constitutes the test of a great general.
plain: The natural shape of the country is the soldier's best ally. But the ability to judge the enemy, to control the forces that bring victory, and to calculate difficulties, dangers and distances shrewdly is the test of a great general.
notes: 'Controlling the forces of victory' may also be read as 'taking control of the victory'.

original: He who knows these things, and in fighting puts his knowledge into practice, will win his battles. He who knows them not, nor practises them, will surely be defeated.
plain: Whoever knows these things and puts that knowledge into practice in battle will win. Whoever does not know them or practise them will surely be defeated.

original: If fighting is sure to result in victory, then you must fight, even though the ruler forbid it; if fighting will not result in victory, then you must not fight even at the ruler’s bidding.
plain: If fighting is sure to bring victory, you must fight, even if the ruler forbids it. If fighting will not bring victory, you must not fight, even if the ruler orders it.
notes: Compare VIII.3 and III.17 (5) on the limits of the ruler's authority over the general.

original: The general who advances without coveting fame and retreats without fearing disgrace, whose only thought is to protect his country and do good service for his sovereign, is the jewel of the kingdom.
plain: The general who advances without seeking fame and retreats without fearing disgrace, whose only thought is to protect his country and serve his ruler well, is the treasure of the kingdom.
notes: 'Coveting' means craving. 'Jewel of the kingdom' means the state's greatest asset. Some translators read 'protect his country' as 'protect the people'.

original: Regard your soldiers as your children, and they will follow you into the deepest valleys; look on them as your own beloved sons, and they will stand by you even unto death.
plain: Treat your soldiers as your children and they will follow you into the deepest valleys. Look on them as your own beloved sons and they will stand by you even to the death.
notes: 'Even unto death' means even to the point of dying.

original: If, however, you are indulgent, but unable to make your authority felt; kind-hearted, but unable to enforce your commands; and incapable, moreover, of quelling disorder: then your soldiers must be likened to spoilt children; they are useless for any practical purpose.
plain: But if you are indulgent but cannot make your authority felt, kind-hearted but cannot enforce your orders, and also unable to stop disorder, then your soldiers are like spoilt children: useless for any practical purpose.

original: If we know that our own men are in a condition to attack, but are unaware that the enemy is not open to attack, we have gone only halfway towards victory.
plain: If we know our own men are ready to attack but do not know the enemy is not open to attack, we have only gone halfway to victory.

original: If we know that the enemy is open to attack, but are unaware that our own men are not in a condition to attack, we have gone only halfway towards victory.
plain: If we know the enemy is open to attack but do not know our own men are not ready to attack, we have only gone halfway to victory.

original: If we know that the enemy is open to attack, and also know that our men are in a condition to attack, but are unaware that the nature of the ground makes fighting impracticable, we have still gone only halfway towards victory.
plain: If we know the enemy is open to attack and that our men are ready to attack, but do not know that the ground makes fighting impractical, we have still only gone halfway to victory.

original: Hence the experienced soldier, once in motion, is never bewildered; once he has broken camp, he is never at a loss.
plain: So the experienced soldier, once on the move, is never confused; once he has broken camp, he is never at a loss.
notes: 'Broken camp' means packed up and set off.

original: Hence the saying: If you know the enemy and know yourself, your victory will not stand in doubt; if you know Heaven and know Earth, you may make your victory complete.
plain: So it is said: if you know the enemy and know yourself, your victory will not be in doubt. If you know Heaven and know Earth, you can make your victory complete.
notes: This echoes III.18 and adds Heaven (weather and season) and Earth (ground) from I.7-8. Some versions read the last word as 'inexhaustible' rather than 'complete'.

original: Sun Tzŭ said: The art of war recognises nine varieties of ground: (1) Dispersive ground; (2) facile ground; (3) contentious ground; (4) open ground; (5) ground of intersecting highways; (6) serious ground; (7) difficult ground; (8) hemmed-in ground; (9) desperate ground.
plain: Sun Tzu said: The art of war recognises nine kinds of ground: (1) dispersive ground; (2) easy ground; (3) contested ground; (4) open ground; (5) crossroads ground; (6) serious ground; (7) difficult ground; (8) hemmed-in ground; (9) desperate ground.
notes: Each name is defined in XI.2-10. 'Facile' means easy; 'contentious' means fought-over; 'ground of intersecting highways' means a crossroads between states. 'Serious' is also rendered 'heavy' or 'deep'. These are situations as much as landscapes.

original: When a chieftain is fighting in his own territory, it is dispersive ground.
plain: When a leader is fighting in his own territory, it is dispersive ground.
notes: 'Dispersive' because soldiers near home are tempted to scatter back to their families. 'Chieftain' means a feudal lord.

original: When he has penetrated into hostile territory, but to no great distance, it is facile ground.
plain: When he has gone into hostile territory, but not far, it is easy ground.
notes: 'Facile' (easy) because retreat is easy - and so is desertion. Also rendered 'light' or 'marginal' ground.

original: Ground the possession of which imports great advantage to either side, is contentious ground.
plain: Ground whose possession gives either side a great advantage is contested ground.
notes: 'Imports' means brings or carries.

original: Ground on which each side has liberty of movement is open ground.
plain: Ground where each side can move freely is open ground.

original: Ground which forms the key to three contiguous states, so that he who occupies it first has most of the Empire at his command, is ground of intersecting highways.
plain: Ground that is the key to three neighbouring states, so that whoever takes it first controls most of the empire, is crossroads ground.
notes: 'Contiguous' means bordering. 'The Empire' means the whole Chinese world of rival states (see III.7).

original: When an army has penetrated into the heart of a hostile country, leaving a number of fortified cities in its rear, it is serious ground.
plain: When an army has gone deep into hostile country, leaving a number of fortified cities behind it, it is serious ground.
notes: 'Serious' is also rendered 'heavy' - deep enough that turning back is hard.

original: Mountain forests, rugged steeps, marshes and fens—all country that is hard to traverse: this is difficult ground.
plain: Mountain forests, rugged slopes, marshes and fens - any country that is hard to get through - is difficult ground.
notes: 'Fens' are low, wet marshland.

original: Ground which is reached through narrow gorges, and from which we can only retire by tortuous paths, so that a small number of the enemy would suffice to crush a large body of our men: this is hemmed in ground.
plain: Ground reached through narrow gorges and left only by winding paths, so that a small number of the enemy could crush a large body of our men, is hemmed-in ground.
notes: 'Tortuous' means twisting. Giles writes 'hemmed in' here without a hyphen and 'hemmed-in' elsewhere; the original is kept.

original: Ground on which we can only be saved from destruction by fighting without delay, is desperate ground.
plain: Ground where we can only be saved from destruction by fighting without delay is desperate ground.
notes: Also rendered 'deadly' or 'death' ground.

original: On dispersive ground, therefore, fight not. On facile ground, halt not. On contentious ground, attack not.
plain: So on dispersive ground, do not fight. On easy ground, do not stop. On contested ground, do not attack.
notes: 'On contentious ground, attack not' is usually read as: do not attack an enemy who already holds it.

original: On open ground, do not try to block the enemy’s way. On ground of intersecting highways, join hands with your allies.
plain: On open ground, do not try to block the enemy's way. On crossroads ground, join up with your allies.
notes: 'Do not try to block the enemy's way' is Giles's reading. Many translators read it as 'do not let your own formations get cut off from each other'.

original: On serious ground, gather in plunder. In difficult ground, keep steadily on the march.
plain: On serious ground, gather plunder. On difficult ground, keep moving steadily.
notes: 'Gather in plunder' means take supplies from the land, since supply lines from home are long.

original: On hemmed-in ground, resort to stratagem. On desperate ground, fight.
plain: On hemmed-in ground, use stratagems. On desperate ground, fight.
notes: Compare VIII.2.

original: Those who were called skilful leaders of old knew how to drive a wedge between the enemy’s front and rear; to prevent co-operation between his large and small divisions; to hinder the good troops from rescuing the bad, the officers from rallying their men.
plain: Those called skilled leaders in the past knew how to drive a wedge between the enemy's front and rear; to stop his large and small units working together; to stop his good troops rescuing the poor ones, and his officers from rallying their men.
notes: 'The good troops' and 'the bad' may also be read as the high-ranking and the low-ranking.

original: When the enemy’s men were scattered, they prevented them from concentrating; even when their forces were united, they managed to keep them in disorder.
plain: When the enemy's men were scattered, they stopped them regrouping; even when the enemy's forces were united, they managed to keep them in disorder.
notes: 'Concentrating' means regrouping or massing together.

original: When it was to their advantage, they made a forward move; when otherwise, they stopped still.
plain: When it was to their advantage, they moved forward; when not, they stayed put.

original: If asked how to cope with a great host of the enemy in orderly array and on the point of marching to the attack, I should say: “Begin by seizing something which your opponent holds dear; then he will be amenable to your will.”
plain: If I were asked how to deal with a large enemy army in good order and about to march to the attack, I would say: 'Start by seizing something your opponent values; then he will do what you want.'
notes: 'Holds dear' is often read as something he depends on - supplies, a key position, or an ally - not only something he loves. 'Amenable to your will' means willing to go along with you.

original: Rapidity is the essence of war: take advantage of the enemy’s unreadiness, make your way by unexpected routes, and attack unguarded spots.
plain: Speed is the essence of war. Take advantage of the enemy's unreadiness, go by unexpected routes, and attack unguarded places.
notes: 'Rapidity is the essence of war' is a strong claim; compare VII.7-8, which warns against forced marches.

original: The following are the principles to be observed by an invading force: The further you penetrate into a country, the greater will be the solidarity of your troops, and thus the defenders will not prevail against you.
plain: These are the principles for an invading force: the further you go into a country, the more united your troops become, and so the defenders will not overcome you.
notes: 'Solidarity' means unity and cohesion.

original: Make forays in fertile country in order to supply your army with food.
plain: Raid fertile country to supply your army with food.
notes: 'Forays' means raids.

original: Carefully study the well-being of your men, and do not overtax them. Concentrate your energy and hoard your strength. Keep your army continually on the move, and devise unfathomable plans.
plain: Look after your men's wellbeing carefully and do not overwork them. Concentrate your energy and save your strength. Keep your army constantly moving and make plans no one can see into.
notes: 'Unfathomable' means impossible to see into or understand.

original: Throw your soldiers into positions whence there is no escape, and they will prefer death to flight. If they will face death, there is nothing they may not achieve. Officers and men alike will put forth their uttermost strength.
plain: Put your soldiers in positions with no way out and they will choose death over flight. If they are ready to face death, there is nothing they cannot achieve. Officers and men alike will give everything they have.
notes: 'Whence' means from which.

original: Soldiers when in desperate straits lose the sense of fear. If there is no place of refuge, they will stand firm. If they are in the heart of a hostile country, they will show a stubborn front. If there is no help for it, they will fight hard.
plain: Soldiers in desperate situations lose their sense of fear. If there is nowhere to escape to, they will stand firm. If they are deep in hostile country, they will put up stubborn resistance. If there is no other choice, they will fight hard.
notes: 'Straits' means difficulties.

original: Thus, without waiting to be marshalled, the soldiers will be constantly on the qui vive; without waiting to be asked, they will do your will; without restrictions, they will be faithful; without giving orders, they can be trusted.
plain: So, without being drilled, the soldiers will be constantly alert; without being asked, they will do what you want; without restrictions, they will be loyal; without being given orders, they can be trusted.
notes: 'On the qui vive' is a French phrase meaning on the alert. 'Marshalled' means organised or drilled.

original: Prohibit the taking of omens, and do away with superstitious doubts. Then, until death itself comes, no calamity need be feared.
plain: Ban fortune-telling and get rid of superstitious doubts. Then, until death itself comes, there is no disaster to fear.
notes: 'Omens' are supposed signs of the future. The last sentence is often read as: the soldiers will not try to escape until they die.

original: If our soldiers are not overburdened with money, it is not because they have a distaste for riches; if their lives are not unduly long, it is not because they are disinclined to longevity.
plain: If our soldiers are not weighed down with money, it is not because they dislike wealth. If their lives are not long, it is not because they do not want to live long.
notes: The meaning is compressed: the soldiers give up wealth and long life, not because they do not care about them. The reason is left implied - the situation of XI.23-24 leaves them no choice.

original: On the day they are ordered out to battle, your soldiers may weep, those sitting up bedewing their garments, and those lying down letting the tears run down their cheeks. But let them once be brought to bay, and they will display the courage of a Chu or a Kuei.
plain: On the day they are ordered into battle, your soldiers may weep - those sitting up wetting their clothes with tears, those lying down letting tears run down their cheeks. But once they are cornered, they will show the courage of a Chu or a Kuei.
notes: 'Bedewing' means wetting. 'Brought to bay' means cornered, with no escape. Chu (Zhuan Zhu) and Kuei (Cao Gui) were famous brave figures of ancient China.

original: The skilful tactician may be likened to the shuai-jan. Now the shuai-jan is a snake that is found in the Ch‘ang mountains. Strike at its head, and you will be attacked by its tail; strike at its tail, and you will be attacked by its head; strike at its middle, and you will be attacked by head and tail both.
plain: The skilled tactician can be compared to the shuai-jan, a snake found in the Ch'ang mountains. Strike its head and its tail attacks you; strike its tail and its head attacks you; strike its middle and both head and tail attack you.
notes: The shuai-jan (shuairan) is a legendary snake; the name suggests 'sudden' or 'swift'. The Ch'ang mountains are Mount Heng. Giles italicised the snake's name; the markers are removed.

original: Asked if an army can be made to imitate the shuai-jan, I should answer, Yes. For the men of Wu and the men of Yüeh are enemies; yet if they are crossing a river in the same boat and are caught by a storm, they will come to each other’s assistance just as the left hand helps the right.
plain: If asked whether an army can be made to act like the shuai-jan, I would say yes. The men of Wu and the men of Yüeh are enemies, yet if they are crossing a river in the same boat and get caught in a storm, they will help each other just as the left hand helps the right.
notes: Wu and Yüeh (Yue) were rival states (see VI.21). The 'same boat' image became a Chinese proverb.

original: Hence it is not enough to put one’s trust in the tethering of horses, and the burying of chariot wheels in the ground.
plain: So it is not enough to rely on tethering the horses and burying the chariot wheels in the ground.
notes: Tethering horses and burying wheels were ways of stopping an army from running away. The point is that physical restraints alone will not hold an army together.

original: The principle on which to manage an army is to set up one standard of courage which all must reach.
plain: The principle for managing an army is to set one standard of courage that everyone must reach.
notes: Some translators read it as 'make everyone brave as one', rather than a standard to be met.

original: How to make the best of both strong and weak—that is a question involving the proper use of ground.
plain: How to get the best out of both the strong and the weak is a question of using the ground properly.
notes: Ground can make weak troops effective and strong troops more so - see Chapter X.

original: Thus the skilful general conducts his army just as though he were leading a single man, willy-nilly, by the hand.
plain: So the skilled general leads his army as if he were leading one man by the hand, whether he likes it or not.
notes: 'Willy-nilly' means whether they want to or not - the soldiers cannot help following.

original: It is the business of a general to be quiet and thus ensure secrecy; upright and just, and thus maintain order.
plain: It is the general's job to be calm and so keep things secret; to be upright and fair and so keep order.
notes: Some translators read the qualities as 'calm and inscrutable, correct and self-controlled' - about the general's manner rather than his fairness.

original: He must be able to mystify his officers and men by false reports and appearances, and thus keep them in total ignorance.
plain: He must be able to mystify his officers and men with false reports and appearances, and so keep them completely in the dark.
notes: A hard line for modern readers: deception aimed at one's own troops. Some translators soften it to 'keep them unaware of his plans'.

original: By altering his arrangements and changing his plans, he keeps the enemy without definite knowledge. By shifting his camp and taking circuitous routes, he prevents the enemy from anticipating his purpose.
plain: By changing his arrangements and his plans, he keeps the enemy from knowing anything for sure. By moving his camp and taking roundabout routes, he stops the enemy from guessing his purpose.
notes: Some versions read 'he keeps the enemy without definite knowledge' as 'he keeps the people (his own men) from understanding'.

original: At the critical moment, the leader of an army acts like one who has climbed up a height and then kicks away the ladder behind him. He carries his men deep into hostile territory before he shows his hand.
plain: At the critical moment, the leader of an army acts like someone who has climbed up high and then kicks the ladder away behind him. He takes his men deep into hostile territory before he shows his hand.
notes: 'Shows his hand' is a card-playing image for revealing his intentions; the Chinese image is releasing a crossbow trigger.

original: He burns his boats and breaks his cooking-pots; like a shepherd driving a flock of sheep, he drives his men this way and that, and none knows whither he is going.
plain: He burns his boats and breaks his cooking pots. Like a shepherd driving a flock of sheep, he drives his men this way and that, and no one knows where he is going.
notes: Burning boats and breaking pots remove any way back. 'Whither' means to where.

original: To muster his host and bring it into danger:—this may be termed the business of the general.
plain: Gathering his army and bringing it into danger - this can be called the general's business.
notes: 'Muster' means gather. 'Host' means army.

original: The different measures suited to the nine varieties of ground; the expediency of aggressive or defensive tactics; and the fundamental laws of human nature: these are things that must most certainly be studied.
plain: The different measures suited to the nine kinds of ground, when to attack or defend, and the basic laws of human nature: these must certainly be studied.
notes: 'Aggressive or defensive' may also be read as 'advancing or withdrawing'. 'Expediency' means usefulness.

original: When invading hostile territory, the general principle is, that penetrating deeply brings cohesion; penetrating but a short way means dispersion.
plain: When invading hostile territory, the general principle is that going deep brings unity, while going only a short way brings scattering.
notes: This restates XI.20 and starts a second pass through the nine grounds (XI.42-50), which partly repeats XI.2-14 - possibly a sign the text was assembled from more than one source.

original: When you leave your own country behind, and take your army across neighbourhood territory, you find yourself on critical ground. When there are means of communication on all four sides, the ground is one of intersecting highways.
plain: When you leave your own country and take your army across neighbouring territory, you are on critical ground. When there are routes in all four directions, it is crossroads ground.
notes: 'Critical ground' is not one of the nine listed in XI.1, which has puzzled commentators. Some translators render it 'cut-off' or 'isolated' ground.

original: When you penetrate deeply into a country, it is serious ground. When you penetrate but a little way, it is facile ground.
plain: When you go deep into a country, it is serious ground. When you go only a little way, it is easy ground.

original: When you have the enemy’s strongholds on your rear, and narrow passes in front, it is hemmed-in ground. When there is no place of refuge at all, it is desperate ground.
plain: When the enemy's strongholds are behind you and narrow passes are ahead, it is hemmed-in ground. When there is nowhere to escape at all, it is desperate ground.

original: Therefore, on dispersive ground, I would inspire my men with unity of purpose. On facile ground, I would see that there is close connection between all parts of my army.
plain: So on dispersive ground I would inspire my men with a single purpose. On easy ground I would make sure all parts of my army stay closely linked.

original: On contentious ground, I would hurry up my rear.
plain: On contested ground I would hurry up my rear.
notes: 'Hurry up my rear' is Giles's literal reading. It may mean bring up the rear quickly to reach the key ground in time, or move round behind the enemy. Commentators disagree.

original: On open ground, I would keep a vigilant eye on my defences. On ground of intersecting highways, I would consolidate my alliances.
plain: On open ground I would keep a close watch on my defences. On crossroads ground I would strengthen my alliances.

original: On serious ground, I would try to ensure a continuous stream of supplies. On difficult ground, I would keep pushing on along the road.
plain: On serious ground I would try to keep supplies flowing. On difficult ground I would keep pressing on along the road.
notes: Compare XI.13 ('gather in plunder'), which tells you to supply the army from the land; this point stresses a continuous supply.

original: On hemmed-in ground, I would block any way of retreat. On desperate ground, I would proclaim to my soldiers the hopelessness of saving their lives.
plain: On hemmed-in ground I would block every route of retreat. On desperate ground I would tell my soldiers there is no hope of saving their lives.
notes: Blocking retreat here is meant to make your own men fight; compare VII.36, where you leave the enemy a way out.

original: For it is the soldier’s disposition to offer an obstinate resistance when surrounded, to fight hard when he cannot help himself, and to obey promptly when he has fallen into danger.
plain: For it is a soldier's nature to resist stubbornly when surrounded, to fight hard when there is no other choice, and to obey promptly when in danger.
notes: 'Disposition' means nature or tendency.

original: We cannot enter into alliance with neighbouring princes until we are acquainted with their designs. We are not fit to lead an army on the march unless we are familiar with the face of the country—its mountains and forests, its pitfalls and precipices, its marshes and swamps. We shall be unable to turn natural advantages to account unless we make use of local guides.
plain: We cannot ally with neighbouring rulers until we know their intentions. We are not fit to lead an army on the march unless we know the lie of the land - its mountains and forests, its traps and cliffs, its marshes and swamps. We cannot turn natural advantages to our benefit unless we use local guides.
notes: Repeats VII.12-14 almost word for word.

original: To be ignorant of any one of the following four or five principles does not befit a warlike prince.
plain: Not knowing any one of the following four or five principles is unworthy of a warlike ruler.
notes: Which 'four or five principles' are meant is unclear - the text does not list them. Some read it as 'any one of these things'. 'Warlike prince' translates a term for a dominant ruler, sometimes rendered 'hegemon'.

original: When a warlike prince attacks a powerful state, his generalship shows itself in preventing the concentration of the enemy’s forces. He overawes his opponents, and their allies are prevented from joining against him.
plain: When a dominant ruler attacks a powerful state, his generalship shows in stopping the enemy's forces from coming together. He overawes his opponents, and their allies are prevented from joining against him.
notes: 'Overawes' means intimidates through superior power.

original: Hence he does not strive to ally himself with all and sundry, nor does he foster the power of other states. He carries out his own secret designs, keeping his antagonists in awe. Thus he is able to capture their cities and overthrow their kingdoms.
plain: So he does not try to ally himself with everyone, nor does he build up the power of other states. He pursues his own secret plans and keeps his opponents in awe. That way he can capture their cities and overthrow their kingdoms.
notes: Some translators read the start as describing the enemy's position: because of the dominant ruler's power, the enemy cannot gather allies. Giles reads it as the dominant ruler's own policy. 'All and sundry' means everyone.

original: Bestow rewards without regard to rule, issue orders without regard to previous arrangements; and you will be able to handle a whole army as though you had to do with but a single man.
plain: Give rewards without regard to the usual rules, and issue orders without regard to earlier arrangements, and you will be able to handle a whole army as if you were dealing with one man.
notes: Debated. It may mean rewarding beyond normal rules in emergencies, or issuing unannounced orders to suit the moment - not arbitrary favouritism. Giles's commentary records disagreement.

original: Confront your soldiers with the deed itself; never let them know your design. When the outlook is bright, bring it before their eyes; but tell them nothing when the situation is gloomy.
plain: Present your soldiers with the task itself; never let them know your plan. When the outlook is good, show it to them; but tell them nothing when things look bad.
notes: 'Confront your soldiers with the deed itself' means give them the job to do without explaining the reasoning.

original: Place your army in deadly peril, and it will survive; plunge it into desperate straits, and it will come off in safety.
plain: Put your army in deadly danger and it will survive; plunge it into desperate trouble and it will come out safe.
notes: Often rendered 'throw them into a place of death and they will live'. The claim depends on XI.23-24.

original: For it is precisely when a force has fallen into harm’s way that is capable of striking a blow for victory.
plain: For it is exactly when a force has got into danger that it is able to strike a winning blow.
notes: Giles's text reads 'that is capable', missing 'it'; the original is kept exactly.

original: Success in warfare is gained by carefully accommodating ourselves to the enemy’s purpose.
plain: Success in war comes from carefully going along with the enemy's purpose.
notes: 'Accommodating ourselves to the enemy's purpose' may mean pretending to go along with his plans, or carefully studying his intentions. Both readings appear in translations.

original: By persistently hanging on the enemy’s flank, we shall succeed in the long run in killing the commander-in-chief.
plain: By sticking persistently to the enemy's flank, we will eventually succeed in killing his commander-in-chief.
notes: Variant reading: 'concentrate on one direction of the enemy, and from a thousand li away kill his general'. Giles's 'hanging on the flank' is one interpretation.

original: This is called ability to accomplish a thing by sheer cunning.
plain: This is called being able to achieve something by pure cunning.
notes: 'Sheer' means pure or nothing but.

original: On the day that you take up your command, block the frontier passes, destroy the official tallies, and stop the passage of all emissaries.
plain: On the day you take command, close the border passes, destroy the official passes, and stop all envoys from coming and going.
notes: 'Official tallies' were split tokens used as travel permits or passes. 'Emissaries' means envoys. Some read 'take up your command' as 'the day the decision to go to war is made'.

original: Be stern in the council-chamber, so that you may control the situation.
plain: Be strict in the council room so that you can control the situation.
notes: 'Council-chamber' is where war plans were decided - possibly the ancestral temple of I.26. Some translators read 'stern' as 'thorough' in deliberation.

original: If the enemy leaves a door open, you must rush in.
plain: If the enemy leaves a door open, you must rush in.

original: Forestall your opponent by seizing what he holds dear, and subtly contrive to time his arrival on the ground.
plain: Get ahead of your opponent by seizing what he values, and quietly arrange the timing of his arrival on the ground.
notes: Compare XI.18. The second half is disputed: it may mean secretly fix a time to meet him in battle, or arrange things so he arrives where and when you want.

original: Walk in the path defined by rule, and accommodate yourself to the enemy until you can fight a decisive battle.
plain: Follow the path set by the rules, and adapt yourself to the enemy until you can fight a decisive battle.
notes: Some translators read it the opposite way: discard the rules and adapt to the enemy. The Chinese word can mean following or departing from a set line.

original: At first, then, exhibit the coyness of a maiden, until the enemy gives you an opening; afterwards emulate the rapidity of a running hare, and it will be too late for the enemy to oppose you.
plain: So at first be as shy as a young woman, until the enemy gives you an opening; then be as fast as a running hare, and it will be too late for the enemy to resist you.
notes: 'Coyness of a maiden' is Giles's phrase - a 1910 image of shy restraint. Some translators render the hare as an 'escaping rabbit'.

original: Sun Tzŭ said: There are five ways of attacking with fire. The first is to burn soldiers in their camp; the second is to burn stores; the third is to burn baggage-trains; the fourth is to burn arsenals and magazines; the fifth is to hurl dropping fire amongst the enemy.
plain: Sun Tzu said: There are five ways of attacking with fire. The first is to burn soldiers in their camp; the second, to burn supplies; the third, to burn baggage trains; the fourth, to burn arsenals and stores; the fifth, to hurl burning material among the enemy.
notes: 'Magazines' means storehouses for weapons or gunpowder - here, stores. The fifth item is disputed: Giles's 'hurl dropping fire' may mean fire arrows or firebombs; others read it as burning the enemy's supply routes or formations.

original: In order to carry out an attack, we must have means available. The material for raising fire should always be kept in readiness.
plain: To carry out an attack, we must have the means. The materials for starting fires should always be kept ready.

original: There is a proper season for making attacks with fire, and special days for starting a conflagration.
plain: There is a right season for fire attacks, and particular days for starting a blaze.
notes: 'Conflagration' means a large fire.

original: The proper season is when the weather is very dry; the special days are those when the moon is in the constellations of the Sieve, the Wall, the Wing or the Cross-bar; for these four are all days of rising wind.
plain: The right season is when the weather is very dry. The particular days are when the moon is in the constellations of the Sieve, the Wall, the Wing or the Cross-bar, because these four are all days of rising wind.
notes: These are four of the 28 'lunar mansions' of Chinese astronomy. The link between them and wind is traditional belief, not modern science.

original: In attacking with fire, one should be prepared to meet five possible developments:
plain: When attacking with fire, be ready for five possible developments:

original: (1) When fire breaks out inside the enemy’s camp, respond at once with an attack from without.
plain: (1) When fire breaks out inside the enemy's camp, respond at once with an attack from outside.

original: (2) If there is an outbreak of fire, but the enemy’s soldiers remain quiet, bide your time and do not attack.
plain: (2) If fire breaks out but the enemy's soldiers stay calm, wait and do not attack.
notes: 'Bide your time' means wait patiently.

original: (3) When the force of the flames has reached its height, follow it up with an attack, if that is practicable; if not, stay where you are.
plain: (3) When the fire has reached its height, follow up with an attack if possible; if not, stay where you are.

original: (4) If it is possible to make an assault with fire from without, do not wait for it to break out within, but deliver your attack at a favourable moment.
plain: (4) If you can make a fire attack from outside, do not wait for fire to break out inside, but attack at a good moment.

original: (5) When you start a fire, be to windward of it. Do not attack from the leeward.
plain: (5) When you start a fire, be upwind of it. Do not attack from downwind.
notes: 'Windward' means upwind; 'leeward' means downwind.

original: A wind that rises in the daytime lasts long, but a night breeze soon falls.
plain: A wind that rises during the day lasts a long time, but a night breeze soon drops.
notes: A traditional weather observation, offered as practical advice.

original: In every army, the five developments connected with fire must be known, the movements of the stars calculated, and a watch kept for the proper days.
plain: In every army, the five developments to do with fire must be known, the movements of the stars calculated, and a watch kept for the right days.

original: Hence those who use fire as an aid to the attack show intelligence; those who use water as an aid to the attack gain an accession of strength.
plain: So those who use fire to help an attack show intelligence; those who use water to help an attack gain added strength.
notes: 'Accession of strength' means an increase in strength. Some translators read the first clause as 'fire attacks are clear in their effect'.

original: By means of water, an enemy may be intercepted, but not robbed of all his belongings.
plain: With water, an enemy can be cut off, but not stripped of everything he has.
notes: 'Intercepted' means cut off - for example by flooding. Fire destroys property; water only blocks.

original: Unhappy is the fate of one who tries to win his battles and succeed in his attacks without cultivating the spirit of enterprise; for the result is waste of time and general stagnation.
plain: Unlucky is the person who tries to win battles and succeed in attacks without following through on them, because the result is wasted time and general stagnation.
notes: Hard to translate. Giles has 'without cultivating the spirit of enterprise'. Many translators read it as: winning battles but failing to secure the gains (or reward the victors) - which is a waste. Some read it as a link to the warning about anger in XII.18.

original: Hence the saying: The enlightened ruler lays his plans well ahead; the good general cultivates his resources.
plain: So it is said: the wise ruler plans well ahead; the good general develops his resources.
notes: 'Enlightened' means wise or clear-sighted. 'Cultivates his resources' may also be read as 'follows the plan through'.

original: Move not unless you see an advantage; use not your troops unless there is something to be gained; fight not unless the position is critical.
plain: Do not move unless you see an advantage. Do not use your troops unless there is something to gain. Do not fight unless the situation is critical.
notes: 'Critical' here means dangerous, demanding action.

original: No ruler should put troops into the field merely to gratify his own spleen; no general should fight a battle simply out of pique.
plain: No ruler should send troops into the field just to satisfy his own anger; no general should fight a battle just out of resentment.
notes: 'Spleen' means bad temper. 'Pique' means irritation from wounded pride.

original: If it is to your advantage, make a forward move; if not, stay where you are.
plain: If it is to your advantage, move forward; if not, stay where you are.
notes: Repeats XI.17.

original: Anger may in time change to gladness; vexation may be succeeded by content.
plain: Anger may in time turn to happiness; annoyance may give way to contentment.
notes: 'Vexation' means annoyance.

original: But a kingdom that has once been destroyed can never come again into being; nor can the dead ever be brought back to life.
plain: But a kingdom once destroyed can never come back into being, and the dead can never be brought back to life.

original: Hence the enlightened ruler is heedful, and the good general full of caution. This is the way to keep a country at peace and an army intact.
plain: So the wise ruler is careful, and the good general full of caution. This is how to keep a country at peace and an army whole.
notes: 'Heedful' means careful. 'Intact' means whole, undamaged.

original: Sun Tzŭ said: Raising a host of a hundred thousand men and marching them great distances entails heavy loss on the people and a drain on the resources of the State. The daily expenditure will amount to a thousand ounces of silver. There will be commotion at home and abroad, and men will drop down exhausted on the highways. As many as seven hundred thousand families will be impeded in their labor.
plain: Sun Tzu said: Raising an army of a hundred thousand men and marching them long distances brings heavy losses on the people and drains the state's resources. Daily spending will reach a thousand ounces of silver. There will be upheaval at home and abroad, and men will collapse exhausted on the roads. As many as seven hundred thousand families will be kept from their work.
notes: 'Labor' is American spelling in Giles's text; the original is kept exactly. The 700,000 figure is usually explained by an ancient system in which groups of families supported each soldier.

original: Hostile armies may face each other for years, striving for the victory which is decided in a single day. This being so, to remain in ignorance of the enemy’s condition simply because one grudges the outlay of a hundred ounces of silver in honours and emoluments, is the height of inhumanity.
plain: Opposing armies may face each other for years, fighting for a victory that is decided in a single day. That being so, to stay ignorant of the enemy's situation just because you begrudge spending a hundred ounces of silver on honours and pay is the height of inhumanity.
notes: 'Emoluments' means payments or salaries. 'Inhumanity' because ignorance prolongs war and costs lives.

original: One who acts thus is no leader of men, no present help to his sovereign, no master of victory.
plain: Anyone who acts like this is no leader of men, no real help to his ruler, and no master of victory.

original: Thus, what enables the wise sovereign and the good general to strike and conquer, and achieve things beyond the reach of ordinary men, is foreknowledge.
plain: So what lets the wise ruler and the good general strike and win, and achieve things beyond ordinary people, is foreknowledge.
notes: 'Foreknowledge' means knowing in advance - here, intelligence about the enemy. Giles italicised it; the markers are removed.

original: Now this foreknowledge cannot be elicited from spirits; it cannot be obtained inductively from experience, nor by any deductive calculation.
plain: This foreknowledge cannot be got from spirits. It cannot be worked out by comparing past experience, nor by any calculation.
notes: Giles's 'inductively from experience' and 'deductive calculation' are his 1910 philosophical labels. The Chinese more likely means: not by analogy with past events, and not by astrological calculation. Translators vary.

original: Knowledge of the enemy’s dispositions can only be obtained from other men.
plain: Knowledge of the enemy's positions can only be got from other people.
notes: Often read as 'from people who know the enemy's situation'.

original: Hence the use of spies, of whom there are five classes: (1) Local spies; (2) inward spies; (3) converted spies; (4) doomed spies; (5) surviving spies.
plain: Hence the use of spies, of which there are five kinds: (1) local spies; (2) inside spies; (3) converted spies; (4) doomed spies; (5) surviving spies.
notes: Each kind is defined in XIII.9-13. 'Inward' means inside - officials within the enemy. Other renderings: 'double agents' for converted, 'expendable' or 'dead' spies for doomed, 'living' spies for surviving.

original: When these five kinds of spy are all at work, none can discover the secret system. This is called “divine manipulation of the threads.” It is the sovereign’s most precious faculty.
plain: When all five kinds of spy are at work, no one can uncover the secret system. This is called 'the divine handling of the threads'. It is the ruler's most precious ability.
notes: The 'threads' image is Giles's; the Chinese is often rendered 'divine organisation' or 'spirit-like web'.

original: Having local spies means employing the services of the inhabitants of a district.
plain: Having local spies means using the people who live in a district.
notes: Some texts read 'local spies' as 'native spies' or 'village spies'.

original: Having inward spies, making use of officials of the enemy.
plain: Having inside spies means using officials of the enemy.

original: Having converted spies, getting hold of the enemy’s spies and using them for our own purposes.
plain: Having converted spies means getting hold of the enemy's spies and using them for our own purposes.
notes: These are what we would now call double agents.

original: Having doomed spies, doing certain things openly for purposes of deception, and allowing our own spies to know of them and report them to the enemy.
plain: Having doomed spies means doing certain things openly in order to deceive, letting our own spies know about them, and having them report them to the enemy.
notes: They are 'doomed' because when the deception is discovered, the enemy is likely to kill them. The spies may not know the information is false.

original: Surviving spies, finally, are those who bring back news from the enemy’s camp.
plain: Surviving spies, finally, are those who come back with news from the enemy's camp.

original: Hence it is that with none in the whole army are more intimate relations to be maintained than with spies. None should be more liberally rewarded. In no other business should greater secrecy be preserved.
plain: So no one in the whole army should be kept on closer terms than spies. No one should be more generously rewarded. In no other business should greater secrecy be kept.
notes: Giles's sentence leaves unsaid with whom the 'intimate relations' are kept; it is usually read as the commander.

original: Spies cannot be usefully employed without a certain intuitive sagacity.
plain: Spies cannot be used well without a certain intuitive wisdom.
notes: 'Sagacity' means wisdom or shrewd judgement. Some translators render it 'sageliness' - the wisdom of a sage.

original: They cannot be properly managed without benevolence and straightforwardness.
plain: They cannot be managed properly without kindness and straight dealing.
notes: 'Benevolence' see I.9. Others render the pair as 'humanity and justice'.

original: Without subtle ingenuity of mind, one cannot make certain of the truth of their reports.
plain: Without a subtle, ingenious mind, you cannot be sure their reports are true.

original: Be subtle! be subtle! and use your spies for every kind of business.
plain: Be subtle! Be subtle! And use your spies for every kind of business.

original: If a secret piece of news is divulged by a spy before the time is ripe, he must be put to death together with the man to whom the secret was told.
plain: If a spy reveals a secret before the time is right, he must be put to death, together with the person he told.
notes: A harsh rule from an ancient setting; stated without softening in the text.

original: Whether the object be to crush an army, to storm a city, or to assassinate an individual, it is always necessary to begin by finding out the names of the attendants, the aides-de-camp, the door-keepers and sentries of the general in command. Our spies must be commissioned to ascertain these.
plain: Whether the aim is to crush an army, storm a city or assassinate a person, you must always start by finding out the names of the attendants, aides, door-keepers and sentries of the general in command. Our spies must be given the task of finding these out.
notes: 'Aides-de-camp' means a commander's personal assistants. 'Sentries' are guards.

original: The enemy’s spies who have come to spy on us must be sought out, tempted with bribes, led away and comfortably housed. Thus they will become converted spies and available for our service.
plain: Enemy spies who have come to spy on us must be found, tempted with bribes, led away and given comfortable lodging. That way they become converted spies, available for our use.

original: It is through the information brought by the converted spy that we are able to acquire and employ local and inward spies.
plain: It is through the information the converted spy brings that we can recruit and use local and inside spies.

original: It is owing to his information, again, that we can cause the doomed spy to carry false tidings to the enemy.
plain: It is also through his information that we can get the doomed spy to carry false news to the enemy.
notes: 'Tidings' means news.

original: Lastly, it is by his information that the surviving spy can be used on appointed occasions.
plain: And finally, it is through his information that the surviving spy can be used at the appointed times.

original: The end and aim of spying in all its five varieties is knowledge of the enemy; and this knowledge can only be derived, in the first instance, from the converted spy. Hence it is essential that the converted spy be treated with the utmost liberality.
plain: The whole purpose of spying, in all five kinds, is knowledge of the enemy, and this knowledge can only come in the first place from the converted spy. So the converted spy must be treated with the greatest generosity.
notes: 'Liberality' means generosity.

original: Of old, the rise of the Yin dynasty was due to I Chih who had served under the Hsia. Likewise, the rise of the Chou dynasty was due to Lü Ya who had served under the Yin.
plain: In the past, the rise of the Yin dynasty was due to I Chih, who had served under the Hsia. Likewise, the rise of the Chou dynasty was due to Lü Ya, who had served under the Yin.
notes: I Chih (Yi Zhi, also Yi Yin) and Lü Ya (Lü Shang, also Jiang Ziya) were famous ministers who knew a ruling dynasty from the inside and helped the next one overthrow it. Hsia, Yin and Chou are the Xia, Shang (Yin) and Zhou dynasties. Whether they were 'spies' is a matter of interpretation.

original: Hence it is only the enlightened ruler and the wise general who will use the highest intelligence of the army for purposes of spying and thereby they achieve great results. Spies are a most important element in war, because on them depends an army’s ability to move.
plain: So only the wise ruler and the able general will use the most intelligent people in the army for spying, and so achieve great results. Spies are a vital part of war, because an army's ability to move depends on them.
notes: 'The highest intelligence of the army' means the cleverest people available, not military intelligence as an organisation.
